Yichen’s expression remained composed.

“The cut wasn’t finished.”

“Then you should have waited.”

“I know.”

His father looked at him for another moment.

Then he checked his watch.

“I have to go.”

Xiaoran looked at the man.

He had arrived late.

He was leaving before the players had even finished packing up.

Mr. Zhou nodded to her.

“Xiaoran.”

“Good evening, Uncle Zhou.”

“Good evening.”

He turned back to Yichen.

“Keep training.”

Then he left.

He hadn’t said well played, or asked how university was going. One observation, a reminder to keep training, and then his back going out through the gate.

None of them spoke.

Yuhao was the first to break the silence.

“Well.”

Meilin gave him a warning look.

He closed his mouth.

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

His face was unreadable.

She wasn’t sure whether he was disappointed, irritated, or used to it.

“Yichen?”

He adjusted the strap of his bag.

“Hm?”

“Do you want to go?”

He nodded.

“Let’s go.”

She reached for his hand.

He took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was noisy.

Yuhao complained about the restaurant’s portion sizes. Meilin accused him of ordering too much. Xiaoran tried to steal a piece of food from Yichen’s bowl, and he moved it away just far enough to make her protest.

For a while, everything returned to normal.

But Xiaoran noticed that Yichen was quieter than usual, even for him.

But there were moments when she caught him looking at his phone without actually doing anything, or staring at the table while Yuhao told a story.

Eventually, Meilin and Yuhao started arguing about an old high-school incident.

Xiaoran leaned closer to Yichen.

“Are you okay?”

He held her gaze.

“Yes.”

She studied his face.

“Really?”

He smiled slightly.

“Really.”

She didn’t push.

Instead, she slipped her hand beneath the table and found his.

He looked down.

Then his fingers closed around hers.

After a moment, he leaned toward her.

“Don’t worry.”

She looked at him.

“I’m not.”

His expression suggested he didn’t believe her.

She gave his hand a small squeeze.

“I just wanted to hold your hand.”

His gaze softened.

“All right.”

He brought her hand to his lips and kissed her knuckles beneath the table.

Across from them, Yuhao was still talking.

Meilin noticed.

She smiled to herself and returned to her food.

They walked home together after dinner.

The summer evening was warm, the streets illuminated by shop signs and the occasional passing motorcycle. Yuhao had gone in the opposite direction, while Meilin had been picked up by her parents.

Xiaoran and Yichen took the longer route.

They passed the old primary school, the small park, and the bakery street where she had once got hopelessly lost trying to buy him pastries.

Yichen carried both their bags.

Xiaoran walked beside him, occasionally brushing her shoulder against his.

After a while, she asked, “Did you know your father was coming?”

“No.”

She nodded.

“Did you want him to?”

Yichen was quiet.

Then he said, “It doesn’t matter.”

Xiaoran looked up at him.

It wasn’t quite an answer.

But she understood that he wasn’t ready to give her a different one.

She looked ahead.

“Your pass wasn’t bad.”

He studied her.

“What?”

“The pass. In the fourth quarter.”

He gave her a faint smile.

“You don’t have to defend me.”

“I’m not defending you.”

“Then?”

“I’m telling you what I saw. You saw the opening. You made the pass. Your teammate wasn’t ready. It happens.”

Yichen’s gaze returned to the road.

“That’s why it’s a mistake.”

“Yes.”

She said it so plainly that he looked at her again.

She smiled.

“You’re allowed to make mistakes, you know.”

He laughed.

“Thank you for the permission.”

“You’re welcome.”

They walked a little further.

Then he said, “He was right.”

Xiaoran turned toward him.

“About the pass?”

“Yes.”

She nodded.

“Then you can work on it.”

He considered her.

“That’s it?”

“What else?”

“Nothing.”

She smiled.

“You’re very good at basketball, Yichen. That doesn’t mean you can’t improve.”

He was quiet.

Then he reached down and took her hand.

“I know.”

She leaned against his arm.

After a moment, she asked, “Are you disappointed?”

He considered the question.

“Not about the game.”

She waited.

He didn’t elaborate.

She didn’t ask him to.

Instead, she lifted their joined hands and swung them gently between them.

“Come on.”

“Where?”

“Home.”

He looked down at her.

Then he smiled.

“All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that night, Yichen returned to his room after showering.

His basketball bag sat beside his desk.

He took out his shoes, towel, and water bottle, placing each item where it belonged. Then he checked his phone.

There was a message from his father.

Dad: Review the fourth-quarter footage if you can get it.

Yichen looked at the message.

A few seconds later, another one arrived.

Dad: Your footwork is better than at the invitational.

He read it twice. His father hadn’t been at the invitational. He must have found the footage.

He typed a short reply.

Yichen: I’ll review it.

He put the phone down.

Across the room, an old drawer stood slightly open. Inside were school certificates, photographs, a few medals, and things he hadn’t looked at in years.

He pushed it shut.

Then he returned to his desk, opened his laptop, and searched for the game footage.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next afternoon, Xiaoran found him at the small basketball court behind the community center.

She had expected him to be there.

He was alone, wearing a dark training shirt, shooting from the perimeter.

The ball hit the rim.

He retrieved it.

Took another shot.

This time, it went in.

Xiaoran stood by the fence, watching him for a while before calling out.

“Excuse me.”

He turned.

His expression softened when he saw her.

“You’re here.”

“Am I interrupting?”

“No.”

She walked over, holding a plastic bag.

“I brought something.”

He glanced at it.

“What?”

“Food.”

“For me?”

“For you. I ate mine on the way.”

He laughed.

She placed the bag on the bench.

“Your mother said you might be here.”

He looked at her.

“She told you?”

“She asked me to bring you something.”

He shook his head, smiling.

Xiaoran took out a small container.

“Fruit.”

“Thank you.”

“And a sandwich.”

“Thank you.”

“And—”

“Xiaoran.”

She stopped.

He looked at her, amused.

“What else?”

She took out a small packet of tissues.

“You’re welcome.”

He laughed and accepted it.

She sat on the bench while he finished a few more shots.

After a while, he came over, drinking water.

“How long have you been here?”

“Long enough.”

“Watching?”

“Yes.”

“Did I play well?”

She tilted her head.

“Do you want an honest answer?”

“Always.”

“You do a little bounce on your toes before you shoot when you’re annoyed. You did it four times.”

He stared at her.

Then his mouth curved.

“Who taught you that?”

“Me. I don’t watch the ball. I watch you.”

“Impressive.”

She smiled proudly.

He sat beside her.

For a while, they ate in comfortable silence.

Then Xiaoran looked at him.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Last night you told me it doesn’t matter.”

He didn’t answer.

“You don’t have to tell me everything straight away. Just don’t say it doesn’t matter and then come out here on your own the next day.”

He looked at the hoop, and then at her. Then he lifted her hand and pressed a kiss against her fingers.

“I’ll remember.”

She nodded.

“Good.”

He leaned back against the bench.

The court was quiet, with only the occasional sound of a ball bouncing from the far end.

After a while, Xiaoran rested her head against his shoulder.

“By the way.”

“Hm?”

“You’re playing again next week?”

“Probably.”

“Then I’ll come.”

“All right.”

“And Meilin and Yuhao.”

He closed his eyes.

“Do we have to invite Yuhao?”

She laughed.

“Yes.”

“Unfortunate.”

“He cheered for you.”

“He shouted at the wrong time.”

“That’s because he’s enthusiastic.”

“He’s loud.”

“Same thing.”

Yichen smiled and kissed the top of her head.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, when Yichen returned home, he found his father in the study.

Mr. Zhou was reading through some documents.

Yichen stood at the door.

“Dad.”

His father looked up.

“Yes?”

“About yesterday.”

Mr. Zhou put down his pen.

Yichen entered and stood across from the desk.

“The pass was early.”

His father nodded.

“I know.”

“I saw the cut, but I didn’t wait for him to finish.”

Mr. Zhou watched him.

“Then you know what to correct.”

“Yes.”

A brief silence followed.

Yichen looked at his father.

“Did you watch the whole game?”

Mr. Zhou’s expression remained neutral.

“Most of it.”

“You arrived during the third quarter.”

“I had something to attend to.”

Yichen nodded.

His father returned his gaze to the documents.

“Your mother said you’re staying here for the summer.”

“Yes.”

“Don’t neglect your training.”

“I won’t.”

“Good.”

That was the end of the conversation.

Yichen left the study.

He didn’t expect anything more.

But as he walked down the corridor, he heard his father’s voice again.

“Yichen.”

He stopped and turned.

Mr. Zhou was still seated behind the desk.

“Your defense has improved.”

Yichen looked at him.

A small pause.

“Thank you.”

His father nodded once.

Yichen returned to his room.

✦ ✦ ✦

A few days later, Xiaoran found herself in Yichen’s room while he was downstairs.

She had come over to return a book, and his mother had told her she could leave it on his desk.

The room looked much the same as she remembered. Neat, quiet, with everything in its place.

She put the book down.

Then she noticed an old metal box on the shelf, a little dusty, with a faded basketball sticker on the lid. The lid wasn’t quite shut. When she reached up to push it closed, a photograph slid out onto the shelf.

A boy of about twelve in a jersey far too big for him, holding a small trophy in a school gym. In the front row of the stands behind him, Mrs. Zhou was waving with both hands.

Xiaoran smiled and laid the photograph back on top of the medals inside.

When Yichen came upstairs, he found her sitting on the edge of his bed.

“Your book’s on the desk.”

“Thank you.”

He glanced at the shelf, then at her.

“Did you find something?”

“You at twelve. In a jersey like a dress. Your mom was in the front row.”

“She came to everything.”

“And your dad?”

He took the box down and closed the lid properly.

“He never had time.”

He said it the way people mention the weather, and she didn’t ask again.

Instead, she smiled and held out her hand.

“Come here.”

He walked over, taking her hand.

She pulled him down beside her.

“You’re very handsome.”

He glanced at her.

“That’s unrelated.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you telling me?”

“Because I want to.”

He smiled and leaned down to kiss her forehead.

“All right.”

She rested against him.

Downstairs, his mother called them for dinner. Neither of them moved until she called twice.

chapters.desc: Three years together, and Lin Xiaoran has never once seen Zhou Yichen watch basketball. Until 8 AM on a Saturday.
chapters.title: The Terrifying Discovery That Zhou Yichen Was a Nerd
chapters.epigraph: “It’s not nerd things. It’s an organized binder.”
chapters.content:
For almost three years, Lin Xiaoran believed she understood Zhou Yichen completely. Basketball. Business major. Good grades. Annoyingly handsome. Secret softie. Simple. Reasonable. Normal. Then one Saturday morning, she discovered a side of him that genuinely frightened her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It began because Xiaoran was bored. She had claimed one corner of Yichen’s sofa at eight in the morning, supposedly to study, and was mostly drawing pandas in the margins of her media theory notes. Yichen sat at the other end with his laptop. Peaceful. Normal. Then the laptop let out a roar—a full arena of people screaming at once. Xiaoran looked up.

“…What was that?”

“Hm?”

“That.”

Yichen glanced at the screen. “Oh. The game started.”

“What game? It’s eight in the morning.”

“It’s eight in the evening in New York.”

She stared at him. “You get up at eight on a Saturday to watch basketball?”

“Sometimes seven.”

“You never told me.”

“You never asked.”

Fair. Annoyingly fair. She already knew he loved basketball. Everyone knew. She had watched him play for three years, held his jacket through tournaments, researched potassium for him. But she had never once seen him watch it. So she climbed across the sofa and sat beside him, curious. That was her first mistake.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the screen, players ran up and down a court under blinding lights while two commentators talked very fast. Xiaoran understood the basics: ball, hoop, tall men. Then she noticed something horrifying. Yichen was paying attention. Not casual attention, not background-noise attention. The kind of focus he usually reserved for his own games, elbows on his knees, eyes moving across the whole court instead of following the ball. One play ended in a missed shot. Immediately—

“He should have switched.”

Xiaoran turned slowly. “…What?”

“The big man stayed in drop coverage. That gave the guard the whole pull-up.”

“What.”

“And the weak-side help was late, so the corner was open anyway.”

“What.”

“They’ve been doing it all quarter. His shooting numbers off the dribble are the best in the league this month.”

“WHAT.”

Yichen finally looked at her, and paused, because she was staring at him like he had grown a second head.

“…You know what all of that means?” she asked.

“Hm.”

“ALL of it?”

“Hm.”

She grabbed both his shoulders. “WHO ARE YOU?”

✦ ✦ ✦

It got worse, because once she started asking questions, he answered them.

“How do you know they’ll lose?”

“They’re losing the possession battle. Too many turnovers.”

“The what battle?”

“And their spacing is terrible. Look—four guys on one side of the floor.”

“Yichen, you’re speaking wizard.”

“It’s basketball.”

“It is NOT the basketball I know. The basketball I know is you running around looking handsome and me screaming.”

“That’s also basketball.”

The terrifying part was that he wasn’t even trying. It just came out of him, the way math did, the way finding her in a crowd did. Then, during a commercial break, Xiaoran discovered the bookshelf. Huge mistake. Behind the business textbooks, filling an entire shelf, was a row of thick notebooks with years written on the spines in his neat handwriting, starting from when he was thirteen. She pulled one out. Inside were hand-drawn diagrams—circles and arrows and dotted lines—with notes in the margins. Backdoor cut works if the wing over-helps. Try in practice. Dad says I always pass too early.

Under the notebooks was a shoebox full of ticket stubs from city league games, a dog-eared book called Spacing, Tempo and the Modern Offense, and a binder of printed shot charts with colored highlighter on every page. She held up the binder like evidence in a courtroom.

“What is THIS.”

Yichen glanced over. “Shot charts.”

“You PRINTED them. And HIGHLIGHTED them.”

“It’s easier to see on paper.”

“You did this for FUN?”

“Hm.”

Silence. Her boyfriend was a nerd. An actual nerd. Not a basketball player who happened to be smart—a basketball nerd, with a filing system. Yichen looked confused by her reaction. To him this was obviously normal.

“My dad used to watch games with me,” he said, by way of explanation. “He’d pause the replay and ask what I would’ve done.”

“THAT DOESN’T EXPLAIN THE HIGHLIGHTER.”

He looked at the binder, then at her, then back at the binder, genuinely puzzled about where the problem was.

✦ ✦ ✦

When the game came back, the calm, composed Zhou Yichen disappeared entirely.

“Why would you take that shot? No. NO. There’s twenty seconds on the clock.”

“They just threw the game away.”

Xiaoran stared at him. This man was emotionally invested. Deeply, aggressively invested in a team on the other side of the planet that did not know he existed. Then, in the last minute, one player made a cut so clean the defense didn’t even turn around in time, caught the pass in stride, and laid it in. Yichen sat bolt upright.

“THAT was beautiful.”

Xiaoran had never heard him call anything beautiful except a basketball play of his own, and her. Apparently, now there were three things.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rest of the morning became educational suffering, because every time she asked one question, he answered with a lecture.

“What’s a pick-and-roll?”

Twenty minutes.

“What’s drop coverage?”

Fifteen minutes, with diagrams on the back of her media theory notes.

“Why does everyone keep yelling about spacing?”

Thirty minutes. She regretted that one deeply. When the game finally ended, Xiaoran sat slumped against the cushions, mentally exhausted. Yichen looked perfectly happy.

“…You really love this,” she said.

“Hm.”

Simple answer. But it landed differently, because she rarely saw him like this. Not competitive. Not responsible. Not quietly taking care of everyone around him. Just excited, the way a kid gets excited. A little nerdy.

“I didn’t know,” she said.

“Know what?”

“That you could talk this much.”

He laughed—properly laughed.

“You asked questions.”

“YOU HAD ANSWERS READY. You had DIAGRAMS.”

She leaned against his shoulder anyway, warm and comfortable.

“It’s cute,” she said.

“What is?”

“You. Getting this excited about nerd things.”

“It’s not nerd things.”

“You have a binder.”

“It’s an organized binder.”

“SEE.”

He laughed again, helplessly, and put an arm around her waist. Xiaoran smiled into his shoulder. Three years, and she was still finding new parts of him—especially the parts nobody else got to see.

“Want to watch the game tomorrow?” he asked.

She looked up, suspicious. “Are you trying to convert me?”

“Maybe.”

“Will there be another lecture?”

“Probably.”

“Then no.”

“Understandable.”

But for the rest of the week, Lin Xiaoran kept asking—completely out of nowhere, in the middle of lunch, in the library, once during a movie—“What’s drop coverage again?”

Just to watch Zhou Yichen accidentally turn into a basketball nerd all over again.

chapters.desc: Zhou Yichen says he doesn’t need anything for his birthday. Lin Xiaoran remembers one sentence from three months ago.
chapters.title: Two Tickets to the Garden
chapters.epigraph: “Of course I remembered.”
chapters.content:
For most people, buying Zhou Yichen a birthday gift was difficult, because he already had everything. A family with money. Good grades. Basketball. Expensive watches, expensive shoes, expensive everything. Whenever his birthday came around, he said the same thing.

“I don’t need anything.”

Annoying answer. Especially for Lin Xiaoran, because this year she wanted the gift to matter.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three months before his birthday, she found out what it should be. It was another early weekend morning on his sofa. Since discovering that her boyfriend was secretly a basketball nerd, Xiaoran had become very slightly interested in watching games—not much, just enough to understand when he started speaking wizard. She was eating crackers. He was explaining things nobody had asked about. Normal relationship activities. Then the broadcast cut to a wide shot of the arena: an enormous round ceiling, a sea of people, the court glowing in the middle like a stage.

“That’s the Garden,” Yichen said.

“Hm?”

“Madison Square Garden. New York.” He was quiet for a second. “One day I want to watch a game there.”

Xiaoran looked over, because Zhou Yichen almost never said things like that. He was still watching the screen, completely casual, as if he hadn’t just told her a dream.

“Really?”

“Hm.”

“Why that one?”

“It’s the Garden.”

“That explains nothing.”

He laughed quietly. “The history. The building. The way the crowd sounds.” Then, after a moment, more quietly: “Dad and I used to say we’d go. When I was a kid. He never had the time.”

“Why not now?”

He shrugged. “Season’s during school. Tickets. Flights. Planning.” He said it lightly. “Maybe someday.”

Then he went back to explaining spacing, like the conversation had never happened. Lin Xiaoran remembered every word.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three months later, his birthday arrived. Yichen expected something small. A handmade gift, maybe. Clothes. One of Xiaoran’s chaotic, sincere little presents with a card covered in stickers. Instead she handed him an envelope.

“What is this?”

“Open it.”

He was immediately suspicious, because she looked far too excited. Inside were two tickets. For several seconds, Zhou Yichen’s brain stopped working. He read them, then read them again, then a third time, as if they might rearrange themselves into something more reasonable. New York. Madison Square Garden. A Saturday night in January, during winter break. Two seats, very high up, in a section number that began with a two.

“…Yichen?”

Nothing. He was staring at the tickets like they might disappear.

“What is this,” he finally said, very quietly.

Xiaoran blinked. “…Your birthday gift?”

“No.”

“What do you mean, no?”

“No.” He sounded genuinely stunned. A rare event. “Xiaoran. These are tickets to the Garden.”

“I know.”

“I can read.”

“Good.”

“LIN XIAORAN.”

She started laughing, because he looked so shocked, and the famous calm Zhou Yichen had apparently stopped functioning entirely.

“How,” he said.

So she explained. The prize money from the competition. The freelance video jobs she’d taken on weekends, editing a bakery’s promotional clips and a classmate’s cousin’s wedding. Three months of birthday budget. Learning far more about game schedules and seat maps than she had ever wanted to. Waking up at four in the morning to buy them the minute they went on sale. All because of one sentence on a Saturday morning.

“I wanted to surprise you,” she said.

He didn’t say anything. Suddenly Xiaoran felt nervous. Maybe it was too much. Maybe the seats were too high, or January was a bad time, or he’d rather go with his father, or—Yichen stood up. He walked around the table, pulled her to her feet, and hugged her. Hard. So suddenly that she almost squeaked.

“Yichen?”

He didn’t answer. He didn’t let go, either.

“…Are you okay?”

Then he laughed—soft, disbelieving, almost helpless—against her hair.

“You’re insane.”

“I know.”

“You’re actually insane.”

But he still wasn’t letting go, and that told her everything. Zhou Yichen wasn’t a dramatic person. He didn’t get emotional easily or react loudly. Right now, he looked completely overwhelmed.

“You remembered,” he said quietly.

“Hm?”

“The Garden thing.”

And suddenly she understood. It wasn’t really about the tickets, or New York, or even basketball. It was that she had listened. One random morning, one casual sentence, one small dream he’d said out loud and then put away—and she had remembered.

“Of course I remembered,” she said.

He looked down at her, and for once his calm expression was nowhere to be found. The girl he loved had spent three months working and saving for this, just to make him happy. How was anyone supposed to stay calm after that?

“If someone asked me,” he said, “what the best birthday gift I’ve ever gotten was—”

His hand found hers.

“It would be this.”

Xiaoran looked extremely pleased.

“Better than your car?”

“Yes.”

“Better than your watch?”

“Yes.”

“Better than—”

“Stop comparing yourself to objects.”

She laughed. Then a thought hit her.

“Wait. You’re taking me, right? I bought two.”

He finally smiled—the real one, the one that only showed up for her.

“Obviously.”

He laced his fingers through hers.

“You bought the tickets. The least I can do is take the girl I love to New York to use them.”

For the next three days, Chen Yuhao became extremely tired of hearing Zhou Yichen talk about Madison Square Garden over the phone. This was impressive, because normally talking too much was Xiaoran’s job.

chapters.desc: A week after the Garden tickets, Lin Xiaoran turns up to their third anniversary with two packets of instant noodles. Zhou Yichen notices more than she thinks.
chapters.title: Three Years, Quietly
chapters.epigraph: “We’re together. We had dinner. You’re sitting on my sofa. I don’t see the problem.”
chapters.content:
By the time their third anniversary arrived, Lin Xiaoran had become exceptionally skilled at pretending she wasn’t broke.

It was a skill she had been building since a Tuesday morning in October, when she woke up at four to buy two tickets the minute they went on sale.

She had learned to walk past cafés without looking at the menus. She had become good at saying she wasn’t hungry when her friends suggested ordering dessert. She had discovered that the university cafeteria’s cheapest meal was actually quite acceptable if she added enough chilli oil.

And she had become an expert at refusing Zhou Yichen’s offers to buy her things without making it sound like she was refusing him.

The problem was that Zhou Yichen knew her well.

He noticed things. He noticed that she had stopped ordering her usual milk tea after class. He noticed that she had begun checking prices before choosing what to eat. He noticed that she had once taken a considerable amount of time deciding whether she really needed a new notebook. He also noticed that, whenever he suggested going somewhere, she became interested in staying home.

He hadn’t said anything.

Not yet.

But he was beginning to suspect something.

And today, of all days, she had arrived at his apartment carrying a plastic bag containing two packets of instant noodles.

Yichen opened the door.

He looked at the bag.

Then at her.

“Happy anniversary.”

Xiaoran smiled brightly.

“Happy anniversary!”

He stepped aside to let her in.

She walked past him, took off her shoes, and headed straight for the kitchen.

Yichen closed the door.

“What’s in the bag?”

“Dinner.”

He looked at the plastic bag again.

“That’s dinner?”

“Yes.”

“Interesting.”

She turned around.

“Don’t say it like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re judging my culinary choices.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He followed her into the kitchen.

Xiaoran placed the two packets on the counter with the seriousness of someone presenting a carefully prepared menu.

“Tonight’s special.”

Yichen looked at the packaging.

“Instant noodles.”

“Correct.”

“Two servings.”

“Very good.”

“With what?”

She paused.

Then lifted a finger.

“Eggs.”

He nodded.

“Anything else?”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“Why?”

“Just asking.”

“Green onions.”

“Anything else?”

“You’re asking too many questions for someone who hasn’t offered to cook.”

He smiled.

“All right. I’ll cook.”

She immediately handed him the packets.

“Thank you.”

He looked at her, amused.

It wasn’t that he disliked instant noodles. He had eaten them plenty of times, especially during busy periods at university.

But their third anniversary dinner was apparently going to be prepared in his kitchen with two packets of noodles and whatever ingredients they could find in his refrigerator.

He looked at Xiaoran.

She was already opening the refrigerator, examining its contents.

“Do you have eggs?”

“Yes.”

“Green onions?”

“Top drawer.”

“Vegetables?”

“Some.”

She glanced over her shoulder.

“You’re surprisingly well-stocked.”

“I live here.”

“That’s not a guarantee.”

He leaned against the counter, watching her.

She took out two eggs, a small bunch of green onions, and a container of vegetables.

Then she looked at him.

“Don’t just stand there.”

“What would you like me to do?”

“Wash these.”

He accepted the vegetables.

“Yes, chef.”

She smiled.

“Good assistant.”

The noodles were Xiaoran’s idea.

The decision to eat at his apartment had been hers too. She had told him she wanted something simple, that she didn’t feel like dressing up, and that they had both been busy enough lately without making a big occasion of it.

All of that was true.

What she hadn’t told him was what the tickets had really cost.

He knew about the prize money and the weekend editing jobs. She’d told him at his birthday dinner a week ago, while he was still holding the envelope. She hadn’t told him that the seats had gone up in price on the morning of the sale, or that the difference had come out of everything else: her milk tea, her phone top-up, the new tote bag she’d been going to buy in November, and most of December.

She didn’t regret a single yuan. She just hadn’t expected their third anniversary to arrive one week later.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up.

“Hm?”

“Your noodles are boiling over.”

Her eyes widened.

“Oh!”

She hurried toward the stove.

Yichen moved aside, letting her take over.

“You’re supposed to watch them.”

“I was watching.”

“You were thinking.”

“That’s the same thing.”

“Not when the water is escaping.”

She looked at the pot.

Then at him.

“You’re very talkative today.”

He smiled and handed her the chopsticks.

She stirred the noodles, muttering something about how difficult it was to cook with an audience.

Yichen didn’t tell her that he had already noticed the way she had been calculating expenses in her head whenever they went out.

He didn’t tell her that he had seen her hesitate before buying a drink last week.

And he certainly didn’t tell her that, when she had arrived earlier, he had noticed she was carrying the same old tote bag she had been using for months, even though its strap was beginning to fray.

He had considered asking.

But he had also noticed something else.

She was happy, the plain kind, nothing like the bright show she put on when she wanted to distract him from something.

She had been smiling since she arrived.

And he didn’t want to turn their anniversary into an interrogation.

So he let her stir the noodles.

They ate on his sofa.

The coffee table had been cleared, leaving enough space for two bowls, two pairs of chopsticks, and a small plate of sliced fruit.

Xiaoran had insisted on arranging everything herself.

She had even found two matching glasses for their drinks.

Yichen looked at the table.

“Very elaborate.”

She sat down beside him.

“Don’t underestimate my preparation.”

“I wouldn’t dare.”

She handed him his bowl.

“Happy anniversary.”

He accepted it.

“Happy anniversary.”

They touched their glasses together.

Then Xiaoran took her first bite.

She closed her eyes.

“Mmm.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Good?”

“Very.”

He tasted his own.

“It’s good.”

She smiled proudly.

“See?”

“Although I suspect the chef had something to do with it.”

“Obviously.”

He leaned back against the sofa.

She settled beside him, her legs folded beneath her, and began eating as if it were a banquet.

Yichen watched her.

“You’re hungry.”

She met his eyes.

“Of course. It’s dinner.”

“You could have told me earlier.”

“Why?”

“I could have prepared something.”

She waved her chopsticks.

“This is prepared.”

He smiled.

“All right.”

She continued eating.

After a while, she looked at him.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me.”

“Am I not allowed?”

“You’re making me nervous.”

He tilted his head slightly.

“Why?”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re doing that thing.”

“What thing?”

“Looking at me like you’re trying to figure something out.”

He smiled.

“Maybe I am.”

She looked down at her bowl.

“Don’t.”

“All right.”

He returned to his noodles.

She watched him for a second, then moved a piece of egg from her bowl into his.

He looked down.

“What’s this?”

“Your share.”

“You gave me the bigger piece.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s our anniversary.”

He met her eyes.

“Does that mean I get the bigger piece every anniversary?”

“Of course.”

“That’s a generous tradition.”

“I’m a generous girlfriend.”

“I know.”

She smiled, pleased.

He picked up the egg and ate it.

After dinner, Xiaoran insisted on washing the dishes.

Yichen told her he could do it.

She told him that he had cooked.

He reminded her that she had brought the ingredients.

She said that was hardly a contribution.

Eventually, they compromised.

She washed.

He dried.

It was a familiar arrangement.

Their shoulders occasionally brushed as they worked. Sometimes she passed him a plate without looking, and he took it without needing to ask. When she reached for the dish towel, he handed it to her before she could.

At one point, she turned around too quickly and almost bumped into him.

He caught her by the waist.

“Careful.”

She looked up.

“You’re standing too close.”

“This is my kitchen.”

“That’s not an excuse.”

He smiled.

She remained where she was, his hand still resting at her waist.

Then she lifted her wet hands.

“Don’t.”

He looked at them.

“What?”

“I know what you’re thinking.”

“I’m not thinking anything.”

“You’re going to wipe your hands on me.”

He looked at her.

Then his smile grew.

“That’s a good idea.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed and released her.

She pointed a wet finger at him.

“Don’t you dare.”

He stepped away, still smiling.

She shook her head, returning to the sink.

A few minutes later, he came up behind her and rested his chin on her shoulder.

She leaned back against him.

“Done?”

“Almost.”

He wrapped his arms around her waist.

She rinsed the last bowl and placed it on the rack.

Then she turned within his arms.

“Now?”

“Now.”

She smiled.

He lowered his head and kissed her.

It was a soft kiss at first, familiar and affectionate. She rested her hands against his chest, then slid them around his neck when he kissed her again.

When they separated, she stayed close.

“Three years,” she whispered.

“Three years.”

“That’s quite a long time.”

“Is it?”

She nodded.

“We’ve known each other for so long.”

“Not long enough.”

She turned to him.

His expression was calm, but there was something warm in his eyes.

She smiled.

“That’s a good answer.”

“I thought so.”

She laughed and kissed his cheek.

They returned to the sofa.

Xiaoran curled up beside him, her head resting on his shoulder. Yichen picked up the remote and opened a streaming service.

“What do you want to watch?”

“Something.”

“That’s helpful.”

“Something romantic.”

He turned to her.

“Do you want to watch a romance?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s our anniversary.”

He nodded.

“Reasonable.”

He scrolled through the options.

She watched him for a while before speaking.

“Actually, I don’t mind what we watch.”

He looked over.

“Then why did you say romance?”

“Because I wanted to.”

He smiled and selected a film.

The opening scene began.

Xiaoran settled more comfortably against him, pulling a cushion into her lap.

Yichen put one arm around her shoulders.

For the first twenty minutes, she watched attentively.

Then she started commenting on the characters.

“Why would she believe him?”

Yichen glanced at the screen.

“Maybe she likes him.”

“That’s not a reason to be stupid.”

He laughed.

A little later, she complained about the male lead’s inability to communicate.

“See? This is why people should talk.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“Do you think we communicate well?”

She considered it.

“Most of the time.”

“Most?”

“Sometimes you just look at me.”

“That’s because you usually know what I’m thinking.”

She smiled.

“Not always.”

“Then ask.”

She looked at him.

“All right. What are you thinking now?”

He held her gaze.

“That you’re comfortable.”

She blinked.

“That’s all?”

“And that I like having you here.”

Her expression softened.

She shifted closer, resting her cheek against his chest.

“Me too.”

He kissed the top of her head.

Halfway through the film, Yichen noticed that Xiaoran was scrolling through her phone.

She wasn’t really reading anything.

She opened an app, closed it, checked the time, then returned to the home screen.

He didn’t ask.

A few minutes later, she put the phone down.

Then picked it up again.

He glanced at the screen.

She was looking at a banking app.

Her thumb hovered over something before she locked the phone.

Yichen looked back at the television.

He had seen enough.

She was worrying about money.

He remembered the way she had declined his offer to take her shopping last weekend. The way she had insisted on splitting a meal when he offered to pay. The way she had become interested in cooking at home.

He had a fair idea why. A week ago she had handed him two tickets to the Garden and told him, glowing, about the prize money and the bakery videos. She hadn’t said a word about what came after. He didn’t want to embarrass her by asking.

So he did something else.

He reached for the fruit on the table and offered her a slice.

She held his gaze.

“Thank you.”

He nodded.

A moment later, he asked casually, “Have you been busy lately?”

She blinked.

“With what?”

“Everything.”

“University?”

“Among other things.”

She considered the question.

“Not especially.”

“All right.”

She looked at him.

“Why?”

“Just asking.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re suspicious.”

He smiled.

“Am I?”

“Yes.”

“Then I should be careful.”

She laughed and took another piece of fruit.

He didn’t ask about the banking app again.

A little later, Xiaoran sat up.

“Wait.”

Yichen paused the film.

“What?”

She looked around the living room.

“Did you prepare anything?”

He studied her.

“What kind of thing?”

“For our anniversary.”

He considered her.

“Does dinner count?”

She smiled.

“Yes.”

“Then I prepared dinner.”

“That’s cheating. I brought dinner.”

“I cooked it.”

“With my ingredients.”

“Which I cooked.”

She laughed.

“You’re impossible.”

He leaned back.

“Would you like something else?”

She shook her head quickly.

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

He watched her face.

She smiled.

“Really. I don’t need anything.”

He believed that she meant it.

At least, he believed that she didn’t need something expensive.

But he wondered whether there was something she wanted and was deliberately avoiding.

He didn’t know how to ask without making it sound like he was questioning her financial situation.

So he reached for her hand.

“Then stay here.”

She tilted her head.

“That’s the plan.”

“Good.”

He pulled her gently closer.

She laughed as she settled against him.

At around ten, Xiaoran’s phone rang.

It was Tang Meilin.

Xiaoran answered.

“Hello?”

Meilin’s voice came through immediately.

“Happy anniversary!”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Thank you!”

“Where are you?”

“At Yichen’s.”

“What did you do?”

“Nothing much.”

“Nothing much?”

“We ate.”

“What did you eat?”

Xiaoran glanced at Yichen.

He was looking at the paused film, listening without appearing to listen.

“Instant noodles.”

There was a silence.

Then Meilin said, “You’re joking.”

“No.”

“On your third anniversary?”

“Yes.”

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Did he forget?”

Yichen looked over.

Xiaoran immediately shook her head.

“No! He didn’t forget.”

“Then why are you eating instant noodles?”

“Because we wanted to.”

Meilin sounded unconvinced.

“Are you sure?”

Xiaoran glanced at Yichen again.

He was still looking at her, his expression unreadable.

She smiled.

“Of course.”

Meilin sighed.

“Fine. Enjoy your romantic noodles.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Goodnight.”

“Goodnight. Tell him I said happy anniversary too.”

“I will.”

She ended the call.

Yichen looked at her.

“Meilin?”

“Mhm.”

“What did she say?”

“She thinks we’re strange.”

He smiled.

“She’s not wrong.”

Xiaoran leaned against him.

“She asked why we ate instant noodles.”

“And what did you say?”

“That we wanted to.”

He looked down at her.

“Good answer.”

She smiled.

Then, after a moment, she asked, “Do you think it’s strange?”

“What?”

“Our anniversary.”

He considered the question.

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“Why would it be?”

She shrugged.

“I don’t know. Three years is a long time. People usually do something special.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Is this not special?”

She blinked.

He gestured vaguely toward the room.

“We’re together. We had dinner. You’re sitting on my sofa. I don’t see the problem.”

She smiled.

“You’re making it sound very simple.”

“It is simple.”

He reached over and tucked her hair behind her ear.

“I want to spend today with you. I am.”

She looked at him.

Then she leaned forward and kissed him.

“All right.”

Later, they moved to his bedroom.

Xiaoran wanted to lie down and finish the film on his tablet.

Yichen sat against the headboard, and she settled beside him with her legs across his lap.

He played with her fingers while the film continued.

After a while, she spoke.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“What’s your favorite memory from the past three years?”

He looked down at her.

“That’s difficult.”

“Why?”

“There are too many.”

She smiled.

“Choose one.”

He thought.

“Probably the day we started dating.”

She blinked.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I was waiting for you to say yes.”

She laughed.

“You made me say it first.”

“You said it first all by yourself. I was just holding the umbrella.”

She looked at him with a soft expression.

“I remember.”

He brushed his thumb across her knuckles.

“What about you?”

She thought about it.

There were so many.

The first time he had held her hand. The first time he had kissed her. Their first anniversary, when they had spent almost nothing and somehow ended up with a day she remembered more fondly than many expensive dates.

His birthday a week ago, and the look on his face when he opened the envelope.

“I think...” She smiled. “I like the ordinary days.”

He considered her.

“Why?”

“Because there are so many of them. Special days are nice. Birthdays, anniversaries, holidays. But most of our time isn’t spent doing something special. It’s just... this.”

She gestured toward the room.

“Watching something. Eating. Talking. Sometimes studying. Sometimes doing nothing.”

He smiled.

“And you like that?”

“Very much.”

He leaned down and kissed her forehead.

“Then we’ll have more.”

She studied his face.

“Promise?”

“Promise.”

It was nearly midnight when Yichen walked her to the door.

Xiaoran had put on her shoes and found her keys, and left her tote bag on his sofa without noticing.

She turned toward him.

“Today was nice.”

“Yes.”

“Even though we didn’t do anything.”

“We did plenty.”

“Like what?”

“Eating.”

She laughed.

“That’s not enough.”

“Watching a film.”

“Still not enough.”

“Talking.”

She smiled.

“Better.”

He reached for her waist and pulled her closer.

“Being with you.”

She looked up at him.

“That’s enough.”

He kissed her.

Then her forehead.

Then her cheek.

She rested her hands against his chest.

“Happy anniversary.”

“Happy anniversary.”

She hesitated.

Then said, “I love you.”

His expression softened.

“I love you too.”

She smiled and finally left.

Yichen watched until she disappeared into the elevator.

Then he closed the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found the notebook the next morning.

It had slid out of the tote bag she’d left on his sofa and fallen open at a page headed GARDEN in her round handwriting. He hadn’t meant to read it. He read it anyway.

Competition prize. Bakery clips, four weekends. Wedding edit. Birthday budget. Every line had a number beside it, and the numbers added up to the price of two seats in a section that began with a two.

Under that, in smaller writing, was a second list.

Milk tea: no.
Phone top-up: next month.
New tote: after New York.
New York food: 300 (pretzel??)

He sat down on the sofa with it.

So that was the instant noodles. And the frayed strap, and the milk tea, and the way she checked prices in the canteen as if they might bite. She’d given him the best birthday present of his life and was planning to eat on three hundred yuan for five days in New York.

He felt surprised first, then something warmer, then an ache in his chest he didn’t have a name for.

He closed the notebook, slid it back into the tote bag exactly where it had been, and picked up his phone. The Garden’s website took a while to load. He read about the seats closest to the court, and then about something called a pregame tour. Then he opened his banking app and typed in the amount she had paid, copied from the top of her page.

✦ ✦ ✦

When Xiaoran arrived that evening, Yichen was in the kitchen.

She walked in, placed her bag down, and immediately looked at him.

“Why are you smiling?”

He glanced over.

“Am I?”

“Yes.”

“Maybe I’m happy.”

“Why?”

He turned off the stove.

“Can’t I be happy?”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re suspicious again.”

He laughed.

She walked toward him.

“What are you cooking?”

“Dinner.”

“What kind?”

“Something better than instant noodles.”

She gasped.

“Are you insulting yesterday’s dinner?”

“Never.”

He handed her a plate.

She looked at it.

Then at him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Why are you being so nice?”

He smiled.

“Because it’s Saturday.”

“That makes no sense.”

“Does it need to?”

She studied him.

He looked perfectly normal.

Too normal, perhaps.

But she couldn’t work out what was different.

He placed another plate on the counter and came closer, brushing a strand of hair behind her ear.

“Eat first.”

She glanced up at him.

Then smiled.

“Okay.”

He kissed her forehead.

She didn’t notice his eyes staying on her a second longer than usual, or know that he’d read a page of her notebook that morning. He served her dinner, listened to her talk about her week, and let her believe he hadn’t noticed anything at all.

She had been perfectly happy with the trade. He could see that, and he wasn’t going to take it from her.

Yichen looked at her across the table.

She was telling him a story, her hands flying, about something that had happened in class that week.

He listened.

Smiling.

When she finished, he reached across the table and took her hand.

“What?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me again.”

“I like looking at you.”

Her cheeks warmed.

“That’s not fair.”

He smiled.

“Why?”

“Because I can’t concentrate when you say things like that.”

He laughed.

Then he lifted her hand and kissed her fingers.

“Happy third anniversary, Xiaoran.”

She blinked.

“That was yesterday.”

“I know.”

She smiled.

“Then happy third anniversary, Yichen.”

He held her hand a little longer. He couldn’t wait to see her face in New York. Until then he let her keep her secret, and kept his.

He pretended not to notice, and she pretended instant noodles were all she had wanted. They were both excellent at it.

chapters.desc: Snow, a pretzel the size of her head, and an envelope that makes Lin Xiaoran shout in a Chinatown noodle shop.
chapters.title: New York Before Tip-Off
chapters.epigraph: “The gift was never the money.”
chapters.content:
The day before the game, Lin Xiaoran discovered two things. First, New York was absurdly big. Second, Zhou Yichen was richer than she remembered.

✦ ✦ ✦

The moment they stepped out of the hotel, Xiaoran stopped walking. Completely. It had snowed overnight. The street was a canyon of buildings so tall she had to tip her head all the way back to see where they ended. Yellow taxis honked at nothing. Steam rose out of a grate in the road like the city was breathing. A man walked past carrying a Christmas tree, three weeks after Christmas, as if that were normal.

“…Xiaoran?”

She pointed at everything at once.

“It looks fake.”

“It’s a city.”

“No.” She pointed again, at a building with a gold roof. “It looks like someone built a movie set and forgot to take it down.”

Yichen smiled quietly. Watching her see New York, he decided, was better than seeing it himself. Every five minutes she discovered something new. Every ten minutes she took another photo. Every fifteen minutes she stopped dead in the middle of the sidewalk to stare up at something and got gently steered aside by a New Yorker who did not have time for this. They walked until their faces went numb. They watched skaters go around the rink under a giant gold statue. They shared a hot pretzel the size of Xiaoran’s head, which she declared “a little disappointing but still important.” They got lost twice—once in Central Park, once inside a single department store.

By evening they were sitting in a tiny noodle place in Chinatown, because a long flight and one hotel breakfast had already made Xiaoran homesick for broth, and the conversation finally turned to tomorrow. The game. The reason they had flown halfway around the world.

“I’m excited,” Xiaoran said. “Even though I still only understand half of what’s happening.”

“Hm.”

“You’ll explain.”

“Hm.”

“No lectures longer than ten minutes.”

“…Hm.”

She narrowed her eyes. “Why are you so happy?”

Yichen looked away. Which was already suspicious.

“There’s something I need to tell you.”

Uh oh.

“What happened?”

“Nothing.”

“That sounds like something happened.”

“Not really.”

Then he slid an envelope across the table.

“…What is this.”

“Open it.”

Now it was her turn to be suspicious. Inside were documents. New tickets. Not their tickets—their tickets were safely in her bag, in a plastic sleeve, because she had checked them every hour since Shanghai. These had different section numbers. A lot lower. The row said A. Xiaoran read them twice.

“…Yichen.”

“Hm.”

“These are not our tickets.”

“Hm.”

“These say courtside.”

“Hm.”

She looked up, very slowly.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

There it was—the tone that meant I know exactly what you’ve done. He stayed calm, mostly because he had known this was coming.

“You upgraded them.”

“Hm.”

“You upgraded EVERYTHING.” She flipped through the rest. Courtside seats. A pregame arena tour. Access to watch the teams warm up from the tunnel. “Yichen, I know how much these cost.”

“Hm.”

“I WORKED FOR MONTHS.”

“I know.”

“I SAVED FOR MONTHS.”

“I know.”

The noodle shop owner glanced over from behind the counter. Two tables away, an elderly couple had stopped eating to watch. Then Xiaoran found the actual crime, tucked at the very back: a bank transfer receipt for exactly the amount she had paid for the original tickets. Silence.

“…No.”

Yichen sighed. Yes. This part. Always this part.

“No?”

“No.” She folded her arms. “Absolutely not.”

“Xiaoran.”

“No.”

“Listen first.”

“No.”

He reached across the table and took her hand.

“You gave me the best birthday gift I’ve ever had,” he said. “You worked weekends for it. You saved your competition money. You got up at four in the morning to buy those tickets.”

She stayed quiet.

“And because I know how hard you worked,” he went on, thumb moving over her knuckles, “the last thing I want is for you to spend everything you saved on me.”

That made the argument harder. Much harder.

“The gift was never the money,” he said. “It was that you remembered. That you wanted me here.”

It was exactly the kind of answer Xiaoran couldn’t fight, because he wasn’t brushing her effort aside or replacing it. He understood what it had meant.

“You don’t get it,” she said, quieter.

“Then explain.”

She looked away. “…I wanted to give you something myself.”

There it was. Not the money. The feeling. Yichen lifted her hand and pressed a kiss to her fingers, right there in the noodle shop, in front of the elderly couple, who looked thrilled.

“You did,” he said. “The moment you bought those first tickets, you already did.”

Xiaoran felt her heart give way a little. Then she pointed at him across the noodles.

“You still upgraded everything.”

“Hm.”

“You didn’t have to.”

“I wanted to.”

“Show-off.”

“Hm.”

At least he admitted it. She kept the original tickets anyway. She wasn’t going to use them, but she folded them carefully back into their plastic sleeve and put them in the inside pocket of her coat, where they stayed for the rest of the trip.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, on the arena tour, they walked out of the tunnel onto the empty court. The ceiling rose above them, enormous and round, rows and rows of empty seats climbing toward it in every direction. A lone janitor was polishing the floor. Their guide was saying something about history and famous nights. Xiaoran forgot she was annoyed. Beside her, Zhou Yichen stood at the edge of the court with his hands in his coat pockets, very still, looking like the happiest man on Earth.

Actually—no. The happiest man on Earth wasn’t looking at the court. He wasn’t looking at the ceiling or the banners or the famous floor. He was looking at her. Because somehow, the best part of the whole trip wasn’t the Garden. It was watching Lin Xiaoran see it with him.

chapters.desc: Game day at Madison Square Garden. But first, a fashion crisis on Fifth Avenue.
chapters.title: The Day Lin Xiaoran Wanted to Look Grown-Up
chapters.epigraph: “Not cute. Not pretty. Beautiful.”
chapters.content:
Game day. Saturday. The day the whole trip had been building toward. The day Lin Xiaoran discovered a completely unexpected crisis. The crisis was not basketball. It wasn’t New York, or the fact that she still understood about forty-seven percent of what Yichen said about defensive schemes. The crisis was fashion.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started at breakfast, in a café on Fifth Avenue, where Xiaoran made the mistake of looking out of the window. Every woman who walked past looked effortless. Long wool coats. Leather gloves. Scarves wrapped like they’d been styled for a magazine. Sleek hair, good boots, the kind of confidence that made a gray sidewalk look like a runway. Then Xiaoran looked down at herself. Puffy white jacket. Comfortable jeans. Sneakers. A small panda keychain hanging from her bag.

She looked like a university student. Because she was a university student. But today, for some reason, she suddenly felt very young. Across the table, Yichen looked up from his coffee and noticed her face immediately.

“What happened?”

Xiaoran pointed at a woman outside the window. “Look.”

He looked. “…Okay.”

“She looks like an adult.”

He looked at the woman, then at Xiaoran, then at the woman again.

“I don’t understand the problem.”

“I look like someone’s daughter.”

Yichen nearly laughed. “Xiaoran.”

“No, seriously. Look at her.” Another woman passed—camel coat, red lipstick, coffee in one gloved hand. “She looks sophisticated. I look like I got lost on a school trip.”

That was when he did laugh—a real one—which only made her more offended.

“THIS IS SERIOUS.”

“It isn’t.”

“YICHEN.”

His smile widened. The idea of Lin Xiaoran having an identity crisis on Fifth Avenue was, to him, extremely funny.

Unfortunately, once she decided something, she was impossible. Thirty minutes later they were shopping—not because Yichen suggested it, but because Xiaoran had announced, “I am becoming elegant today,” and apparently this was non-negotiable.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next three hours were chaos. The first dress was too mature. The second was too fancy. The third made her look, in her own words, like she was attending someone’s divorce. The fourth almost worked, except for the sleeves, which had opinions. Yichen followed behind, carrying more and more shopping bags. Patient. Hopelessly supportive.

At one point, a saleswoman smiled at Xiaoran and said, “Your husband is very patient.”

Xiaoran nearly choked. Yichen looked suspiciously pleased. Neither of them corrected her. Then Xiaoran found it. Not too glamorous. Not too grown-up. A soft burgundy knit dress with a simple neckline and long sleeves, warm enough for January, and a long camel coat to wear over it. Feminine without trying too hard. When she looked in the mirror, she paused.

“…Oh.”

The saleswoman smiled. “That’s the one.”

Even Xiaoran couldn’t argue. She looked older, somehow. Softer. More sure of herself. Still herself—just slightly different. Then she looked over at Yichen. Big mistake. He had gone completely silent.

“…Yichen?”

Nothing.

“Yichen?”

The saleswoman smiled knowingly. “Oh.”

Finally he cleared his throat. “…It looks good.”

Short answer. Too short. Which told Xiaoran everything, because Zhou Yichen only got this brief when he was completely compromised. She smiled in triumph. Success. Unfortunately, the next problem appeared at the register. Yichen paying. Again.

“No.”

“Yes.”

“Yichen.”

“Xiaoran.” Then he made his winning argument. “You bought me the Garden. Let me buy you a dress. You got up at four in the morning for those tickets. Let me win one argument this trip.”

Deeply annoying. But sensible. So the dress became Yichen’s purchase, a fact he looked suspiciously happy about for the rest of the afternoon.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, they took a yellow cab to the arena, and the city outside the window was all lights. Inside, the Garden was nothing like the empty building from the tour. It was full and loud and alive, twenty thousand people under that enormous round ceiling, music thumping, the court shining like it was lit from underneath. Their seats were so close to the floor that Xiaoran could hear the players’ sneakers squeak during warm-ups and see the sweat on the referees’ foreheads.

She stood by her seat in the burgundy dress and the new coat, holding her phone, not even taking photos, just looking. Then she caught her reflection in the glass of the scorer’s table. The dress. The coat. Her hair, which she had spent forty minutes on in the hotel bathroom. For once, she didn’t see a girl who had gotten lost on a school trip. She saw a woman.

It felt nice. Then she noticed Yichen looking at her. Again.

“…What.”

Nothing.

“Yichen. What.”

He looked away. Then, quietly—

“You look beautiful.”

Somehow, after years together, it still worked on her every single time. And this time, the way he said it felt different. Not cute. Not pretty. Beautiful. The word stayed with her. Then the lights went down, the crowd roared, and the game began, and the atmosphere changed completely. Even Xiaoran felt it—the pressure, the speed, how much every possession seemed to matter. And beside her, Yichen changed too. He leaned forward, elbows on his knees, eyes moving across the whole floor at once, tracking every screen and rotation the way he did on the sofa at eight in the morning, except now it was right in front of him. Every time a play worked exactly the way he had explained it on the back of her notes, he made a small sound under his breath, like a man watching a magic trick he already knew the secret to and loved anyway.

He looked ridiculously handsome. Xiaoran decided basketball was dangerous. Not playing it—watching someone you love fall in love with it all over again, three feet from the court. Late in the fourth quarter, a player went flying out of bounds after a loose ball and landed in the second row, two seats down. The whole crowd gasped. Yichen shot to his feet with everyone else. Xiaoran wasn’t watching the player.

She was watching him. He looked happier than she had seen him all year. Without thinking, she slipped her hand into his. He glanced down, surprised for half a second. Then he laced their fingers together and turned back to the game, and didn’t let go. The final minutes went by in a roar. The buzzer sounded. Confetti didn’t fall, because it was a regular season game in January, but it felt like it should have.

And standing there together, in the loudest building Xiaoran had ever been in, both of them quietly realized the same thing. Years from now, when they remembered New York, they probably wouldn’t remember the final score. Or who made which shot, or the defensive schemes, or the forty-seven percent. They would remember this. Her first grown-up dress. His inability to stop looking at her. The noise, the lights, the snow waiting outside.

And the hand he didn’t let go of the whole way home.

chapters.desc: A few comments read at 2 AM, two weeks of skipped meals, and a date that ends in a quiet café.
chapters.title: The Day Zhou Yichen Found Out Lin Xiaoran Was Dieting
chapters.epigraph: “Who told you that you needed to change?”
chapters.content:
There were many things Zhou Yichen worried about. Basketball injuries. Exams. Career plans. Whether Xiaoran remembered her student card. Normal, reasonable concerns. One concern had never crossed his mind, because it sounded impossible: Lin Xiaoran dieting. The girl who once ate three desserts on a single date. The girl who considered bubble tea a personality trait. The girl who treated snacks as emotional support. Dieting? Impossible. Which was exactly why he didn’t notice at first.

It started with social media. Again. Always social media.

✦ ✦ ✦

A month earlier, Xiaoran had posted photos from New York: the burgundy dress, the city lights, a version of herself that looked a little more woman than girl. The response was overwhelmingly positive. Some of it wasn’t. Nothing cruel. Nothing dramatic. Just enough.

“She’s pretty but she’d look even better if she lost a little weight.”

“Her face is beautiful.”

“A slimmer figure would be perfect.”

Stupid, unimportant comments—the kind most people would ignore. Except Xiaoran read them at 2 AM, scientifically the worst time to read anything. And somehow they stayed with her. Not because she hated herself. She didn’t. But for the first time, she started wondering: what if? So Lin Xiaoran made a terrible decision. She started dieting, secretly. Not healthy dieting. Not reasonable dieting. Skipping breakfast, tiny lunches, coffee instead of food, water whenever she was hungry—the kind of diet guaranteed to make everyone miserable, especially her.

The strange part was that nobody noticed right away. Xiaoran acted mostly normal, and university was busy—deadlines, projects, practices, exams, life. Even Zhou Yichen missed it, for almost two weeks.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then came Saturday. Date day. The plan was simple: lunch, shopping, walking around the city, dinner. Xiaoran woke up feeling awful. Her stomach had spent two weeks surviving on disappointment and caffeine, and it was finally protesting. Violently. She still said nothing, because she didn’t want Yichen to worry. Terrible decision.

✦ ✦ ✦

By noon the stomachache was worse. Walking hurt. Standing hurt. Existing hurt. Somehow she kept smiling—until Yichen stopped walking.

“Xiaoran, what’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

A terrible lie. She looked pale—very pale—and Zhou Yichen knew her too well.

“No.”

“What?”

“Something hurts.”

Dead silence. Caught. Again.

“…My stomach.”

Everything changed, because Zhou Yichen’s expression changed. Not panic. Not anger. Worry. Always worry first.

“When did it start?”

“A little while ago.”

“How long.”

She hesitated.

“Xiaoran.”

“…This morning.”

The truth, finally. She’d been hiding it all morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ten minutes later they were sitting in a quiet café. A warm drink in front of her. Food in front of her. Food she wasn’t touching. And finally, Yichen actually noticed.

“…Why aren’t you eating.”

Silence. Then more silence.

“…I’m not hungry.”

Wrong answer. Very wrong answer. Suddenly the pieces connected: the smaller meals, the constant coffee, the weight she’d lost, how tired she’d been. Everything. Dead silence.

“Have you been dieting?”

Uh oh. Xiaoran looked away. The universal sign of guilt. Zhou Yichen became angry. Not loud. Not shouting. The worst kind: quiet angry.

“Lin Xiaoran.”

She winced. He had used her full name. Maximum danger.

“Answer me.”

“…A little.”

“A little.”

Xiaoran said nothing.

“You’ve barely been eating for two weeks.”

Oops. Of course he knew. Nothing stayed hidden from him forever.

“Why.”

Suddenly Xiaoran felt stupid. The comments sounded ridiculous now. Embarrassing. Small.

“…I wanted to look prettier.”

The anger disappeared. Completely. That answer hurt worse. Much worse.

“Xiaoran.”

She didn’t look up. Couldn’t. A hand touched her forehead, warm. Then a kiss—right on her forehead, soft and lingering. Xiaoran blinked, confused. She had expected a lecture. Not that.

“Look at me.”

She did. Big mistake. His eyes looked sad. Actually sad. Somehow that was worse than anger.

“Who told you that you needed to change?”

Xiaoran shook her head.

“Don’t do that.”

Another kiss to her forehead, gentle and patient.

“Who.”

“…Nobody.”

A lie. But he let it go. That wasn’t the point. Then another kiss against her forehead. And another. Each one impossibly gentle.

“What am I supposed to do with you?”

His voice sounded helpless.

“Yichen—”

Another kiss.

“You skip meals.”

Kiss.

“You drink coffee instead.”

Kiss.

“You get sick.”

Kiss.

“And somehow you’re surprised your stomach hurts.”

By now, Xiaoran’s ears were red. Being scolded while being repeatedly kissed was very confusing.

“I just wanted to look prettier.”

Then Yichen laughed. His hand moved to hold her cheek, gently.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“You took me to New York. You worked for months to buy those tickets. You won competitions. You make everyone around you happier. And somehow the thing you’re worried about is losing weight?”

She looked down, because it sounded ridiculous when he said it.

“I just…”

Nothing came out. She didn’t even know anymore. Yichen sighed—the sigh he saved for her alone—and pushed the food toward her.

“Eat.”

Xiaoran didn’t move.

“Eat. Or I’m carrying you home.”

He sounded completely serious, which made it believable.

“You won’t think I’m ugly?”

Yichen leaned forward and kissed her forehead again, longer this time, then whispered,

“You’re beautiful when you’re eating. You’re beautiful when you’re studying. You’re beautiful when you’re talking too much. You’re beautiful when you’re annoying.”

“That’s rude.”

“Accurate.”

Then, more seriously: “If comments like that get in your head again, tell me. Don’t fix it by not eating.”

A tiny smile appeared. There she was—the real Xiaoran. Watching her finally pick up her fork made Zhou Yichen more relieved than winning a basketball game. He still spent the rest of the date kissing her forehead every twenty minutes, just to make sure she remembered. And every single time, he quietly added:

“Eat your food.”

Which was considerably less romantic.

chapters.desc: A thirteen-day family vacation. Lin Xiaoran is a mature adult. Day Three is concerning.
chapters.title: Two Weeks Was Apparently Too Long
chapters.epigraph: “I hate family vacations.”
chapters.content:
When Zhou Yichen announced he was leaving on a thirteen-day family vacation, Lin Xiaoran laughed. Actually laughed.

“That’s fine.”

“Hm.”

“I’m a mature adult.”

“Hm.”

“I can survive two weeks.”

“Hm.”

Tang Meilin, who had been there for the One-Week Clingy Disaster of high school, looked deeply suspicious. Whenever Xiaoran claimed she was emotionally stable, disaster usually followed. Day One wasn’t bad at all. Yichen left in the morning. Xiaoran went to class, worked on assignments, had dinner with friends. Perfectly normal. At 10 PM she called him, for three hours. Still normal. Probably. Day Two was manageable. She sent him pictures of lunch, of campus, of a cat near the media building. Then another cat. Then another. Then a cloud that vaguely resembled a cat. Yichen replied: You sent me six cats today.

Xiaoran: You’re welcome.

Day Three was concerning, because after class she walked toward the business building out of habit—then remembered Yichen wasn’t there. He was several countries away. It hit surprisingly hard.

“…Oh.”

For the first time, campus felt a little bigger. A little emptier. Which was ridiculous, because she had survived sixteen whole years before meeting him. Yet somehow the place felt wrong without him. Day Four, things escalated.

“You’re staring at your phone.”

One of her classmates pointed it out.

“I’m not.”

“You checked it six times.”

“I received messages.”

“Not from him.”

Xiaoran had no answer.

Caught. Yichen, meanwhile, appeared to be having the time of his life. At least, that’s what his photos suggested: beaches, resorts, family dinners, mountain views. Every picture looked amazing, which only made Xiaoran more annoyed. How dare he enjoy himself while she suffered? A completely unreasonable thought. But still. Day Five, she stole one of his hoodies. Again. Not because she missed him. Obviously. It just happened to smell faintly like his cologne, which was entirely unrelated.

Day Six, the video calls got longer. Day Seven, even longer. At one point, Mrs. Zhou wandered into the background and laughed.

“Still talking?”

Dead silence. They had been talking for two hours.

“Mom.”

“What?”

Mrs. Zhou looked delighted. She waved at Xiaoran.

“He’s been carrying his phone around all day waiting for your messages.”

Dead silence. Yichen looked horrified.

“Mom. Please leave.”

Xiaoran was trying very hard not to smile. That information was valuable. Very valuable. Day Eight, the suffering peaked. Not dramatically. Quietly.

That afternoon, Xiaoran won a small media competition. Normally Yichen was the first person she’d tell—not because she had to, but because she wanted to. But it was the middle of the night where he was. Suddenly the win felt slightly incomplete, which surprised her. Later that night, his reply arrived. Three words. Proud of you. She stared at them for five minutes. Day Nine, Chen Yuhao called.

“Are you alive?”

“Barely.”

“It’s been nine days.”

“Feels like nine years.”

“You’re impossible.”

“Correct.”

Day Ten, she started counting. Three days left. Then two. Then one. Every conversation somehow included, “When are you coming back?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eventually, even Yichen noticed.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You asked me that six times.”

“I’m just checking.”

“Xiaoran.”

“…Fine. I miss you.”

Silence.

“I know.”

Simple and soft, the kind of answer that made missing him worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

The final day arrived. Thirteen days. Long enough for Xiaoran to decide she hated extended vacations. The airport felt familiar now—she had done this once before, in high school, for one single week. This time she wasn’t dramatic. Not visibly. No clinging, no pouting, no speeches. Just waiting. Patiently. Okay—not patiently. She checked the arrival board twelve times. Finally the doors opened, and there he was. Black shirt. Travel backpack. Slightly messy hair. The same Zhou Yichen—and somehow not, because after almost two weeks, seeing him in person felt strangely unreal.

Then he spotted her and smiled, and just like that, everything felt normal again. Yichen walked toward her.

“Hi.”

Xiaoran threw herself at him. Not gracefully. Not elegantly. Just immediately—hard enough that Yichen took a step back catching her. Her arms tightened, and for a while neither of them said anything. Thirteen days wasn’t forever. But it had been long enough for Xiaoran to realize something: she didn’t just like spending time with Zhou Yichen. He had quietly become part of what made ordinary days feel complete. Finally she muttered into his shoulder,

“I hate family vacations.”

Yichen laughed softly—the familiar laugh, the one she had missed most.

“I noticed.”

His arms tightened around her. Warm. Safe. Home. After a pause, near her ear, he whispered,

“You know… I missed you too.”

Xiaoran hugged him even tighter, which made Zhou Yichen laugh again. Apparently two weeks apart had only made his girlfriend clingier—an outcome that surprised absolutely nobody.

chapters.desc: A lost French couple, a café near campus, and a language Lin Xiaoran forgot to mention.
chapters.title: The Day Zhou Yichen Discovered His Girlfriend Secretly Spoke French
chapters.epigraph: “The same thing she’d been telling him all along—just in a different language.”
chapters.content:
There were many surprising things about Lin Xiaoran. Some were expected: her ability to get lost in places she’d visited twenty times, her talent for creating problems out of nothing, her habit of asking questions like:

“Would you still love me if I became a refrigerator?”

A follow-up, apparently, to the capybara question. Normal Xiaoran behavior. What Zhou Yichen didn’t expect—was discovering she spoke French. Not badly, either. Fluently enough to make people stare. And she had apparently been practicing for months without telling him. The betrayal was unbelievable. It started on a random Saturday. They were having lunch at a café near campus. Nothing unusual. Just a quiet date—until Xiaoran froze.

“Hm?”

Yichen looked up.

“What happened?”

Xiaoran’s eyes widened, and she sat up straighter. Very suspicious. Across the café, a middle-aged French couple stood looking lost—the man holding a map, the woman holding a phone. Xiaoran stood up.

“I’m back in a minute.”

And walked toward them. Yichen blinked. Okay. Probably helping with directions. Then Xiaoran opened her mouth. French came out. Perfect French. Not textbook French, not app French—real, conversational French. Dead silence. Because WHAT. The French couple immediately brightened. A full conversation followed—questions, answers, directions, recommendations, laughing. Zhou Yichen sat there, staring. Who was this woman? That was his girlfriend. Supposedly. Yet somehow she had unlocked an entire language pack without informing him.

The conversation continued for several minutes. Then Xiaoran smiled, said goodbye, came back, sat down, and went straight back to her juice. Like nothing had happened. Dead silence.

Finally Yichen spoke.

“What.”

“What?”

“You speak French.”

“Oh.”

OH? That was the response?

“Since when?”

“Recently.”

“Recently enough to have a whole conversation?”

Xiaoran went quiet.

Caught. A guilty smile appeared.

“A few months.”

Dead silence.

“A FEW MONTHS?”

She had hidden an entire language. Like a criminal.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

Xiaoran looked genuinely confused.

“I wanted to surprise you.”

Mission accomplished. Yichen was absolutely surprised. Then suspicious.

“When did you learn?”

“Every night.”

“Every night.”

“Mhm.”

“You already have assignments. And competitions.”

“Mhm.”

“You already watch random documentaries about things nobody cares about.”

“Mhm.”

“So when exactly did you have time?”

Xiaoran proudly pointed at herself.

“I am gifted.”

“No.”

“Okay maybe I sacrificed sleep.”

“Thought so.”

The truth. It was always sleep deprivation.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eventually the story came out. Months ago, Xiaoran had watched a French film for one of her media courses. Then another. Then another. Then she had become obsessed, which was very on-brand: when Xiaoran liked something, she liked it aggressively. Normal people watched movies. Xiaoran accidentally learned a language. Then Yichen had an idea. His eyes narrowed.

“Say something.”

“What.”

“In French.”

“No.”

“Why.”

“Embarrassing.”

“You were just speaking confidently.”

“That was practical French.”

“This is boyfriend French.”

Yichen refused to let it go. For twenty whole minutes. Until Xiaoran surrendered.

“Fine.”

Very quietly, she said something in French—soft, fast, beautiful, and completely incomprehensible to him.

“What did you say?”

Xiaoran looked away. Very suspicious.

“Nothing.”

“That’s a lie.”

“It’s not important.”

“Xiaoran.”

“No.”

Now he was definitely curious. If she refused to translate, it meant something. After several more minutes of interrogation, she gave up.

“…I said you’re handsome.”

Yichen smiled. Not a big smile. The dangerous one—the one that always caused problems.

“Oh. That’s all?”

“Yes.”

“Only handsome?”

“YICHEN.”

His smile widened. Xiaoran secretly learning French and then using it to compliment him was absurdly adorable. Then he leaned closer.

“Teach me.”

“What?”

“French.”

“No.”

“Why.”

“Because you’ll immediately use it against me.”

Correct. His face confirmed it immediately.

Three weeks later, he had learned enough French to recognize one specific phrase—one Xiaoran muttered while studying, thinking he wasn’t paying attention. Thinking he couldn’t understand. A terrible mistake. He heard it perfectly, and this time he understood.

“Je t’aime.”

I love you. Simple. Soft. Unconscious. The kind of thing she probably didn’t realize she’d said out loud. Then Yichen closed his textbook.

“What.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“What?”

“You love me?”

Xiaoran froze. No. NO. He wasn’t supposed to understand that yet. Yichen looked unbearably pleased. From that day on, whenever Xiaoran forgot herself and slipped into French, Yichen paid very close attention. His girlfriend had spent months on French, and the first important thing she had learned to say was the same thing she had been telling him all along. Just in a different language.

chapters.desc: A peaceful Saturday at the Zhou house, until Mrs. Zhou’s best friend’s daughter walks in calling him “ge.”
chapters.title: The Worst Visitor in Zhou Family History
chapters.epigraph: “The real problem had always been Xiaoran’s own imagination.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran wasn’t nervous. She had visited the Zhou family house several times already. Mrs. Zhou liked her. Mr. Zhou liked her. Even the neighbors’ cat that slept on the Zhou family wall liked her. Everything was fine. Then Jiang Meimei arrived, and nothing was fine anymore. The disaster started on a Saturday afternoon. Xiaoran was curled up beside Zhou Yichen on the living room sofa, stealing his snacks. Mrs. Zhou was chatting happily, Mr. Zhou was reading, and Yichen was pretending to study. Life was peaceful.

Then the front door opened. Mrs. Zhou brightened at once.

“Oh! Meimei is here!”

Dead silence. Who? The answer appeared five seconds later. A girl walked into the living room—beautiful, elegant, perfect posture, perfect makeup, perfect smile. The kind of woman who had clearly never tripped over her own feet. Unlike Xiaoran, who had once gotten lost inside a shopping mall. Twice.

“Hello Auntie.”

The girl smiled sweetly. Mrs. Zhou immediately hugged her.

“Meimei!”

Uh oh. Xiaoran’s instincts went off like an alarm.

Then came the fatal sentence.

“Xiaoran, this is Jiang Meimei,” Mrs. Zhou said with a smile. “She’s my best friend’s daughter.”

Dead silence. BEST FRIEND’S DAUGHTER? That phrase alone carried terrifying power.

“Meimei practically grew up with Yichen.”

Dead silence. WHAT. Xiaoran slowly turned toward her boyfriend. Yichen looked completely normal, which made it worse. He clearly wasn’t surprised. Meaning he already knew her. Meaning they had history. Meaning—

“Yichen ge.”

Jiang Meimei smiled. Ge. The dreaded honorific.

Meanwhile Yichen simply nodded.

“Meimei.”

HE KNEW HER NAME. Xiaoran sat up straighter. This was serious. Then the conversation started, and somehow everything got worse.

“Oh, Yichen ge, are you still playing basketball?”

“Yes.”

“I saw your tournament photos.”

“Mm.”

“I showed them to my parents.”

“Mm.”

Their families were connected. Xiaoran hated everything. Jiang Meimei sat elegantly across from them, perfect in every way. The killing blow. Mrs. Zhou laughed.

“You know, when they were children, everyone thought Meimei and Yichen would become a couple.”

Xiaoran nearly inhaled a potato chip wrong. Jiang Meimei laughed politely. Mrs. Zhou laughed. Mr. Zhou laughed. Even the cat on the wall looked suspicious. Only Yichen looked exhausted—he had clearly heard this story a thousand times. Xiaoran had not, and now she was suffering. Greatly.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next hour was torture—not because Jiang Meimei did anything wrong. That was the problem. She was nice. Kind, polite, friendly, impossible to dislike. Which made Xiaoran dislike the situation even more. Then, over tea, Jiang Meimei casually mentioned—

“I still have the birthday gift Yichen gave me years ago.”

A birthday gift. HE BOUGHT HER GIFTS. Xiaoran was spiraling. Internally. Externally she was smiling—a very normal smile. Definitely not dying. A hand landed on her knee—warm, steady. Yichen. Without even looking at her, he squeezed once. A warning. He could apparently feel the jealousy radiating off her. Traitor. The real disaster happened later. Mrs. Zhou asked Yichen to help carry something upstairs, and Xiaoran was left alone with Jiang Meimei.

The moment he was gone, panic set in. Now they would have to talk. Woman to woman. Nightmare. Jiang Meimei smiled. Xiaoran prepared for battle. Then, unexpectedly, Meimei laughed.

“You look terrified.”

“…What?”

“You’ve been staring at me for two hours.”

Caught. Immediately. Meimei smiled again, genuinely amused.

“You’re much cuter than I expected.”

“…Expected?”

“Mrs. Zhou talks about you constantly.”

“She does?”

“All the time.”

Then Meimei leaned closer.

“And honestly, I understand now.”

Xiaoran blinked. What was happening? Meimei laughed again.

“You know, Yichen ge never liked any girls growing up. Never.”

“…Really?”

“Really.”
