Then she pointed upstairs.

“The fact he looks at you the way he does is honestly shocking.”

Now Xiaoran wanted details. Many details.

“What way?”

Meimei stared at her, then burst out laughing.

“Oh my God.”

“What?”

“You don’t know.”

Know what? Before Xiaoran could ask, footsteps sounded on the stairs. Yichen was back, and both girls immediately looked at him—one amused, one confused. Yichen looked instantly suspicious.

“…What happened?”

“Nothing,” Jiang Meimei said.

“Nothing,” Xiaoran said, in exactly the same tone. Very dangerous.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, after Jiang Meimei finally left, Xiaoran cornered her boyfriend.

“What way?”

Yichen blinked.

“What.”

“Jiang Meimei said you look at me differently.”

Realization, followed immediately by annoyance. Meimei had started problems on her way out. Wonderful. Yichen sighed.

“Forget it.”

“No.”

“Please.”

“NO.”

Several minutes of relentless pestering later, he finally surrendered.

“The way someone looks at the person they love.”

Direct hit. Xiaoran froze completely. Yichen looked away, slightly embarrassed. Xiaoran scooted closer. Then closer. Then rested her head on his shoulder, smiling.

“Okay.”

“Okay?”

“I’ve decided.”

“What.”

“I don’t hate Jiang Meimei anymore.”

“…You hated her?”

“Briefly.”

“Why.”

“She was too pretty.”

Yichen laughed. And just like that—the greatest threat in Lin Xiaoran’s imagination was over—mostly because Jiang Meimei had never been a rival at all. The real problem had always been Xiaoran’s imagination, which, unfortunately for everyone involved, was far more dangerous.

chapters.desc: Lunar New Year at her grandparents’ house, and one uncle with opinions about why she’s dating Zhou Yichen.
chapters.title: The One Thing Lin Xiaoran Could Never Tolerate
chapters.epigraph: “I chose him because he’s Zhou Yichen.”
chapters.content:
There were many things Lin Xiaoran disliked. Early classes. Group projects. Spicy food stronger than her tolerance, which was most spicy food. People who walked slowly in crowded places. But there was one thing she genuinely hated: gold diggers. Not because she was rich. She wasn’t. Her family lived comfortably—her mother an accountant, her father an engineer—not wealthy, not poor. Enough for food, for school, to get through a month without worrying. Nothing more, nothing less.

So it always made Xiaoran uncomfortable when people assumed she was dating Zhou Yichen for his money—especially since she had liked him long before she knew how wealthy his family actually was. Not everyone understood that. Including Uncle Deng: a distant relative from another city, the kind who appeared once every few years and somehow had opinions about everyone’s lives. It happened at Lunar New Year, at her grandparents’ house. Lots of relatives, lots of food, lots of noise, lots of gossip. A normal family gathering—until someone mentioned Zhou Yichen.

Everyone became very interested.

“That’s the boyfriend in the business program at Huaining University, right?”

“Very handsome.”

“Excellent grades.”

“Good family.”

It was harmless—until Uncle Deng laughed and said, casually,

“Well, Xiaoran certainly found herself a rich boyfriend.”

The room quieted slightly. Xiaoran paused.

“Smart girl,” Uncle Deng went on. “Nowadays girls know how to choose.”

Dead silence. No. Not that. Not that. Across the table, her mother frowned and set down her cup with a small, sharp click. Uncle Deng didn’t notice. Or didn’t care.

“Honestly, if I were young again, I’d choose someone wealthy too.”

A few relatives looked uncomfortable. The implication was very obvious. Xiaoran hated it. Not because it embarrassed her—because it insulted everything she felt for Yichen. Every late-night study session, every tournament, every argument, every moment, reduced to money. Xiaoran put down her chopsticks. Quietly.

“Uncle, if Yichen wasn’t rich, I’d still date him.”

The room went silent. Everyone knew that tone. The dangerous Xiaoran tone. Uncle Deng laughed.

“Of course you’d say that.”

Xiaoran smiled. It was not a friendly smile.

“Actually, when we started dating, I didn’t know his family was wealthy.”

Silence.

“He was just annoying.”

Several cousins burst out laughing. Accurate.

“He studied with me. He helped me. He listened to me complain. He stayed beside me when I failed things. He celebrated when I succeeded.”

Then she looked directly at Uncle Deng.

“So no. I didn’t choose him because he’s rich.”

The room got quieter. Nobody was joking anymore.

“I chose him because he’s Zhou Yichen.”

Dead silence. Even her grandmother looked moved. Uncle Deng looked a little embarrassed, but still tried to defend himself.

“I wasn’t criticizing you.”

“Maybe not,” Xiaoran replied. “But it sounded like you were criticizing him.”

That surprised everyone. Most people would have defended themselves first. Xiaoran defended Yichen first. Always. Without thinking.

“You know what bothers me?”

Nobody answered.

“People think money is why someone stays.”

Her fingers tightened slightly around her teacup.

“But I’ve seen people with money treat others terribly. And I’ve seen people with nothing give everything.”

Then she smiled. A small smile. The real one this time.

“Yichen just happens to have both.”

Her grandmother laughed first.

“That’s a good answer.”

The tension broke. Conversation resumed, food returned, and the family gossip moved on.

Later that evening, as Xiaoran walked home, her phone rang. Yichen.

“Hm?”

“Lin Jun told me what happened.”

Family networks were terrifying.

“What part?”

“The part where you defended my honor.”

Then she heard him laughing softly.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“No, tell me.”

“I just think it’s nice.”

Xiaoran rolled her eyes.

“It wasn’t nice.”

“It was.”

“He was being annoying.”

“And?”

“And nobody gets to talk about you like that.”

A softer silence, the kind Yichen only ever had around her.

“So if I lost everything tomorrow…”

“No.”

“What?”

“No hypothetical questions.”

“Answer.”

She sighed. Then finally said:

“If you lost everything tomorrow, I’d still be there.” Then she added: “Unfortunately.”

Yichen laughed—a real laugh, the kind she loved most. Somehow it felt worth more than all the money in the world.

chapters.desc: Grandma Lin wants to see the boy up close. Uncle Deng will be there. So will the dumplings.
chapters.title: Zhou Yichen Meets the Relatives
chapters.epigraph: “That one’s acceptable.”
chapters.content:
The invitation came from her grandmother, which meant nobody could refuse it.

Three days after Uncle Deng’s comment at New Year dinner, Grandma Lin called Xiaoran’s mother, and Xiaoran’s mother called Xiaoran into the kitchen, and said, without turning around from the sink, “Your grandmother wants the boy at dinner on the fifth.”

Xiaoran froze with a mandarin halfway to her mouth.

“…The boy?”

“Zhou Yichen.”

“Why?”

“She says if you’re going to defend someone in front of the whole family like that, she wants to see what he looks like up close.” Her mother turned off the tap. “Your uncle will be there.”

“Uncle Deng?”

“He’s staying until the seventh.”

Xiaoran put the mandarin down. “Mom. That’s a trap.”

“It’s dinner,” said Mrs. Lin, which in her language meant yes, and you’re both walking into it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen arrived at five, exactly on time, which Xiaoran had known he would. What she hadn’t expected was how he arrived. No black car. He came up the lane from the bus stop on foot, in a plain dark coat, carrying a fruit basket in one hand and a paper bag in the other. Inside the bag were a tin of good tea for her grandfather, a box of pastries from the old bakery near their high school, and a small pot of narcissus for her grandmother, because Xiaoran had once mentioned, months ago and only once, that her grandmother liked them.

She met him at the gate.

“You took the bus.”

“Hm.”

“You never take the bus.”

He looked at the house—the red couplets on the door, the paper lanterns, the sound of a dozen relatives talking over a television—and then back at her.

“Your uncle thinks I’m a rich boyfriend,” he said. “I didn’t want to give him a parking space to prove it.”

Xiaoran stared at him. Then she reached up and fixed the collar of his coat, which didn’t need fixing, mostly so she’d have something to do with her hands.

“You’re nervous,” she said.

“Very.”

That surprised her so much she forgot to be nervous herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside, it was exactly as bad as she’d feared and also completely different. Her grandmother took one look at the narcissus and said “Hm,” in a tone Xiaoran had only ever heard her use for very good melons. Her father shook Yichen’s hand for too long and then had to go stand in the kitchen for a minute. Lin Jun, lounging on the sofa with a beer, raised it in Yichen’s direction like they were old war buddies, which, after the day he’d “stolen” him, they sort of were.

Then the questions started. The aunties wanted to know his height, his major, his grades, and whether he could cook. The uncles wanted to know what business he planned to go into and whether he’d thought about the civil service. Two small cousins wanted to know if he could dunk, and when he said yes, they wanted proof, immediately, in the courtyard, and had to be held back by the hoods of their jackets.

Yichen answered all of it. Calmly. Politely. Without once mentioning his family’s company, or his car, or anything he owned. When one auntie asked what his parents did, he said “My father runs a business, and my mother keeps him from working too much,” and the auntie laughed and moved on. Across the room, Uncle Deng watched all of this over his teacup and didn’t say anything. Xiaoran watched Uncle Deng.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened at the dumpling table. Every year on the fifth, the whole family folded dumplings together, and every year it was a competition nobody admitted was a competition. Grandma Lin sat at the head of the table, folding perfect pleated dumplings at terrifying speed. Xiaoran’s were lopsided but sealed. Lin Jun’s were somehow perfect, which was annoying. Yichen’s were a disaster. He held the wrapper like it was an exam question. He put in too much filling. He pinched the edges with enormous concentration, and the dumpling burst at the seam and lay there on the board, looking injured.

One of the little cousins burst out laughing. So did Grandma Lin.

“Again,” she said, and pushed another wrapper toward him.

He tried again. It was worse.

“You’re better at basketball,” Xiaoran told him.

“I’m better at everything than this.”

Uncle Deng put down his teacup.

“Must be strange,” he said, “doing things with your own hands for once.”

The table didn’t go silent, exactly. But it got quieter. Xiaoran felt her mother go still beside her. She opened her mouth.

Under the table, Yichen’s knee touched hers. Wait. He picked up a third wrapper.

“It is,” he said. “My dad says money is the easiest thing to have and the easiest thing to lose. He made me work in one of his warehouses the summer I was fifteen so I’d understand that.” He spooned in less filling this time. “I was bad at that too. For the first week.”

Uncle Deng raised his eyebrows.

“And,” Yichen added, still looking at the dumpling, “Xiaoran told me what she said to you at New Year.”

Now the table really did go quiet.

“I’m not sure I’ve earned all of it yet,” he said. “But I’m trying to.”

He pinched the edges closed. It held. Grandma Lin picked it up, turned it over, and put it on the tray with her own.

“That one’s acceptable,” she announced.

Across the table, Uncle Deng looked at Yichen for a long moment. Then he picked up his teacup again, and said, gruffly, to nobody in particular, “Too much filling’s a common mistake.”

It was the closest thing to an apology anyone in the family had ever heard from him.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner, the cousins dragged everyone out into the courtyard for sparklers. The air smelled like gunpowder and cold. Somewhere down the lane, someone was setting off firecrackers, and the little cousins screamed and ran in circles, writing their names in light. Xiaoran stood by the door with Yichen, holding a sparkler she’d forgotten to light.

“You didn’t have to say that,” she said. “About earning it.”

“I meant it.”

“I know. That’s why you didn’t have to say it.”

He didn’t answer. He just took her sparkler, lit it from his own, and handed it back. Behind them, the door opened. Xiaoran’s mother came out, wrapped in her coat, holding something red. She walked straight up to Yichen and held out an envelope. He looked at it. Then at Xiaoran. Then back at the envelope, completely lost.

“Auntie, I can’t—”

“Take it,” said Mrs. Lin. “It’s New Year.”

He took it with both hands, the way you were supposed to, and bowed. Mrs. Lin nodded once, brisk as always, and went back inside without another word. Yichen stared at the red envelope in his hands.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm.”

“What does it mean? When the parents give it to—” He stopped.

Xiaoran looked at the door her mother had just closed, at the warm light behind the paper lanterns, at the shape of her grandmother at the window pretending not to watch. She knew exactly what it meant. In her family, the first red envelope from her mother didn’t go to friends, or classmates, or a boy someone was dating for now. It went to someone they expected to see at this table next year. And the year after that.

“It means,” she said, and her voice wobbled, “you have to come back next year and fold better dumplings.”

He looked at her for a long time in the flickering light. Then he tucked the envelope carefully into the inside pocket of his coat, over his heart, and didn’t say anything at all. He didn’t have to.

chapters.desc: A weekly viewing report, eleven hours of dramas, and the most dangerous thing Zhou Yichen has ever done: change a password.
chapters.title: Netflix vs Zhou Yichen
chapters.epigraph: “You violated my human rights.”
chapters.content:
There were many ways to start a relationship conflict. Jealousy. Miscommunication. Trust issues. Different life goals. Lin Xiaoran and Zhou Yichen managed to have one over Netflix—specifically, because Zhou Yichen accidentally found out how much Netflix Xiaoran watched in a single day. The discovery happened on a Tuesday. Yichen paid for the subscription. Not because Xiaoran couldn’t—because he’d insisted.

“Just use mine.”

At the time, Xiaoran thought that was sweet. A mistake.

One afternoon, Yichen got a notification: weekly viewing activity. Normally he ignored those. This time, he opened it—and froze.

“…What?”

The watch history went on. And on. Episodes one through seven of one show. Then another show. Then another. Dead silence. According to Netflix, Lin Xiaoran had spent almost eleven hours watching dramas on Sunday. Eleven. Hours. Yichen messaged her.

Yichen: How many hours were you on Netflix Sunday?

Seen. Typing. Stopped typing. Typing again.

Xiaoran: Why.

Yichen: Answer the question.

Xiaoran: Approximately.

Yichen: How many.

Xiaoran: The number isn’t important.

The number was important.

Yichen: Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: …

Yichen: Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: Maybe.

Yichen: Maybe?

Xiaoran: Nine?

Yichen: The report says eleven.

Dead silence. She had forgotten Netflix tracked things. Traitors, all of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen showed up at her apartment holding groceries, concern, and judgment.

“Eleven hours?”

“It was a weekend.”

“Eleven hours.”

“It sounds worse when you say it.”

“Because it is worse.”

Xiaoran crossed her arms.

“It was educational.”

“What was educational?”

“The romance.”

“No.”

“The character development.”

“No.”

“The cinematography.”

“No.”

Dead silence. Then Yichen opened her refrigerator and discovered she had skipped lunch. The atmosphere got much worse. After the diet incident, skipped meals were the one thing he never joked about.

“Xiaoran. You skipped meals.”

“I forgot.”

“You remembered fourteen episodes.”

Xiaoran had nothing to say to that.

Then came the betrayal. The greatest betrayal.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Netflix logged her out. Because what? WHAT? She tried again. Nothing. Again. Nothing. Then her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Temporary restriction.

Xiaoran stared at the screen.

Xiaoran: You did WHAT?

Yichen: One week.

Xiaoran: ONE WEEK?

Yichen: You need sunlight.

Xiaoran: I HAVE SUNLIGHT.

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: I SAW SUNLIGHT THROUGH THE WINDOW.

Yichen: That’s not the same thing.

The war began. For the first time in months, Lin Xiaoran ignored Zhou Yichen completely. No messages. No calls. No random photos. No good morning, no good night. Nothing. Yichen lasted exactly six hours before he got uncomfortable. Normally his phone held three cat photos, two random observations, one complaint, five unrelated thoughts, and at least one look at this cloud. Today: nothing. The silence was deeply unsettling. Evening came. Still nothing. The next day, nothing. Day three, nothing. By then, even Chen Yuhao had noticed.

“What did you do?”

“I blocked Netflix.”

“You idiot.”

“She watched eleven hours.”

“That’s not the point.”

“Then what’s the point?”

“You touched her freedom.”

Yuhao shook his head.

“She’s going to hold this grudge forever.”

A terrifying possibility.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen found Xiaoran in the media building working on an assignment. She looked up, saw him, and looked straight back down. The audacity.

“Xiaoran.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

Nothing. Finally Yichen sat down beside her, close enough that their shoulders touched. Still ignored. Five minutes passed. Then ten. Finally, Yichen sighed.

“Are you done?”

“No.”

Her first words in three days. Progress.

“You’re really angry.”

“Correct.”

“It was for your health.”

“You violated my rights.”

Her rights. Netflix had apparently become a legal issue. Then Xiaoran turned—actually turned—and pointed at him.

“I was three episodes away from the confession.”

“The confession?”

“Three episodes.”

The heartbreak in her voice almost made him laugh. Almost. Yichen rubbed his forehead. The whole argument was ridiculous.

“I was worried.”

Her anger wavered. That tone was unfair—the genuine one, the honest one.

“You skipped meals. You slept at three.”

More silence.

“You watched until your eyes hurt.”

Xiaoran looked away. Caught. Again.

“I know.”

The fight lost all momentum. The truth was, she knew. And Yichen knew she knew. After a moment, he took out his phone, opened Netflix, changed the password, and handed it over.

“…Really?”

“Really.”

Her anger vanished. Completely. Like magic. Traitorous woman. She grabbed his sleeve—the universal sign of peace.

“Thank you.”

“Conditions.”

“What.”

“No eleven-hour marathons.”

Xiaoran said nothing.

“Xiaoran.”

“Ten?”

“No.”

“Nine?”

“No.”

“Eight?”

“No.”

She leaned her head on his shoulder. The ultimate negotiating strategy, and unfortunately the most effective one, because Zhou Yichen immediately knew he had already lost. Just like every other argument with Lin Xiaoran.

“Six hours maximum,” he said.

Xiaoran gasped.

“Victory.”

“That’s not a victory.”

“It is to me.”

Then she smiled—the bright one, the one that made Yichen forgive things far too easily. As she happily logged back into Netflix, Yichen realized blocking her had been a mistake. Not because she was angry—because a drama-deprived Lin Xiaoran was much harder to handle than a drama-addicted one. A lesson he never repeated.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran is “extremely busy.” Her lie lasts approximately three minutes.
chapters.title: The World’s Worst Liar
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody who was actually busy sent updates about how busy they were.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran was many things. Cute. Dramatic. Smart. Chaotic. A good liar was not one of them. The problem wasn’t that she couldn’t make up stories. She absolutely could. The problem was that Zhou Yichen knew her far too well, which was why her latest lie lasted approximately three minutes. A personal record. The disaster started on a Wednesday afternoon. Yichen had practice. Normally Xiaoran waited for him afterward. Today she wasn’t there. Instead, he got a message.

Xiaoran: I’m busy.

Dead silence. The message already looked suspicious. Not busy with what. Not talk later. Just: I’m busy. Then another message arrived.

Xiaoran: Extremely busy.

Yichen smiled. Nobody who was actually busy sent updates about how busy they were.

An hour later, he found her at the campus café, looking very guilty. The moment she saw him, she sat up straight. Too quickly. Like a criminal.

“Hi.”

“Hi.”

Silence. Yichen sat down across from her—calm, patient—and waited. Eventually, Lin Xiaoran always confessed. She simply couldn’t help herself. And right on schedule, she started talking.

“Today was productive.”

“Oh?”

“Very productive.”

“Hm.”

“I was studying.”

The first lie. Tiny, harmless. But Yichen noticed—not because of the words, but because she tugged her sleeves down over her hands, the way she had for years whenever she was nervous.

“Very serious studying.”

“Hm.”

“Educational.”

“Hm.”

“Academic.”

“Hm.”

Yichen’s mouth twitched. Now she was overexplaining. Another sign. Xiaoran kept talking, and the more she talked, the worse it got.

“I definitely wasn’t doing anything strange.”

There it was: the self-report. Nobody had accused her of anything, and she was already defending herself. Yichen was enjoying himself enormously. Watching Xiaoran lie was one of life’s simplest pleasures—not because she was convincing, but because she wasn’t. At all.

“I spent the entire afternoon being responsible.”

“Responsible.”

“Very.”

“Hm.”

“I would never waste time.”

Now Yichen had to look away, because his smile was becoming noticeable. Xiaoran noticed anyway. Uh oh. She knew that smile—the one that appeared whenever he caught her doing something ridiculous. And suddenly she was flustered. Not because she’d been caught. Because he looked unfairly handsome. There was something deeply dangerous about Zhou Yichen when he knew something she didn’t know he knew. Relaxed, confident, amused—the slight smile, the calm eyes, the feeling that he was letting her dig her own grave and enjoying every second. A disaster.

Yichen leaned back, comfortable, watching.

“So. What exactly were you studying?”

Dead silence. Details. The enemy of every liar. Xiaoran panicked.

“Media.”

“What part?”

“…Media media.”

Yichen’s smile widened, just slightly, and somehow that made her heart beat faster. Not because of the interrogation. Because he looked ridiculously attractive. This was terrible.

“Which assignment?”

“The assignment.”

“Which one?”

“The… important one.”

“Hm.”

The smile grew, slowly, until Xiaoran wanted to hide under the table. Not from embarrassment. From him. Why was he looking at her like that? Yichen folded his arms, still smiling, still patient, very obviously entertained.

“Xiaoran.”

“What.”

“Look at me.”

“No.”

Yichen laughed, which made things worse. He leaned forward, close enough that she could see the amusement in his eyes.

“Why not?”

“Reasons.”

“What reasons?”

“Personal reasons.”

“Such as?”

He was enjoying this far too much. Xiaoran pointed at him.

“Stop smiling.”

“What smile?”

THAT smile. The teasing one, the one that showed up whenever he felt completely in control. Which was unfortunately right now. Yichen tilted his head, still smiling, still impossible, and asked quietly,

“How long were you watching dramas?”

Direct hit. There it was. The truth. And the worst part? He had known from the very first sentence. The entire conversation had been a trap. A cruel, cruel trap. Xiaoran covered her face, defeated.

“Four hours.”

“Hm.”

“Maybe five.”

“Hm.”

“…Six.”

Exactly the six-hour limit from the Netflix treaty. Technically she hadn’t even broken the rule. She had just lied about getting close to it, which was somehow more embarrassing. There it was. The confession. As always. Yichen laughed softly—victorious, annoyingly handsome—and Xiaoran peeked through her fingers, only to regret it immediately. He was still smiling at her like that. Still far too attractive for someone who had just interrogated her.

He reached over and gently moved her hands away from her face.

“Hi.”

Xiaoran groaned.

“I don’t like you.”

“Liar.”

The worst part was that he was right about that, too.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran has discovered a new research topic. It has categories, lists, and ratings. Zhou Yichen would like it to stop.
chapters.title: The Internet Was a Mistake
chapters.epigraph: “Do you know how dangerous you are?”
chapters.content:
There were many things Zhou Yichen feared. Basketball injuries. Losing important tournaments. Lin Xiaoran attempting to cook without supervision. But one thing caused problems more consistently than all of them: the internet. Every time Xiaoran discovered a new interest online, everyone suffered. This week’s victim was Zhou Yichen. It started on a Thursday evening. Yichen was studying. Peacefully. Productively. A rare event. Then his phone vibrated.

Xiaoran: Question.

Every message that started with “Question” was dangerous.

Yichen: What.

Xiaoran: Did you know there are different types of kisses?

Dead silence.

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: There are SO MANY.

Yichen: Why are you researching this.

Seen. No reply. Which was somehow more alarming.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next day, Yichen found out why. Xiaoran showed up outside his lecture hall carrying a notebook. Not suspicious normally. Extremely suspicious when carried by Lin Xiaoran.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“I have information.”

“About?”

“Kisses.”

Dead silence. Several students nearby walked away. Smart people. Xiaoran opened the notebook. It had notes. NOTES.

“Look.”

Yichen looked, and immediately regretted it. She had clearly spent hours on this. There were categories. Lists. Observations. Ratings.

“Why.”

“Educational purposes.”

“No.”

“Fine. Curiosity.”

At least that was honest. Xiaoran pointed at the page.

“Apparently there are forehead kisses.”

“You know that.”

“You do those.”

“Correct.”

“Cheek kisses.”

“You know that too.”

“Hand kisses.”

Yichen didn’t answer.

“Eskimo kisses.”

Then she flipped another page.

“And French kisses.”

Dead silence. There it was. The real reason. Yichen understood everything. He closed the notebook, slowly.

“No.”

“What.”

“No.”

“You haven’t even heard my proposal.”

“I don’t need to. I know exactly where this conversation is going.”

He was right.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three hours later, in a quiet corner of the campus garden, Xiaoran was still talking about it. Relentlessly.

“Why does it have that name?”

“I don’t know.”

“Who invented it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Why is it famous?”

“Xiaoran. Please stop interviewing me.”

She pouted. It had absolutely no effect. Mostly. She rested her chin on his shoulder, thinking. Dangerous.

“I think couples probably try different things naturally.”

Yichen sensed disaster approaching. Rapidly. Xiaoran looked up—curious, innocent, hopelessly unaware.

“…Do you?”

Sometimes Yichen wondered how one person could be so smart and so clueless at the same time. She could analyze media campaigns, win competitions, research anything—and still completely fail to understand the effect she had on him. Very softly, Yichen sighed.

“Xiaoran, do you have any idea what you do to me?”

“What does that mean?”

Exactly. She didn’t know. Not even slightly. He reached over and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear—a familiar gesture that made her smile right away.

“There.”

“There what?”

“That smile.”

“…What about it?”

“You do things like that. You ask questions. You get curious. Then you look at me like everything is simple.”

Xiaoran blinked, completely confused. Yichen laughed quietly. Of course she was. Then he leaned in and kissed her forehead—gentle, warm, familiar. The kiss he always gave her, the one that calmed her down every time.

“There.”

“What was that for?”

“Because I like that one.”

Xiaoran smiled again.

“So that’s a no?”

“Absolutely.”

“This relationship has no freedom.”

Yichen actually laughed—a real laugh, the kind she loved hearing. Xiaoran leaned against him, happy. The internet might have introduced her to dozens of kinds of kisses, but her favorite was still the simplest: Zhou Yichen looking at her like she was the best thing that had ever happened to him, and kissing her forehead like he was quietly reminding himself she was real. Even if she occasionally came up with terrifying research topics.

chapters.desc: In his dream, Lin Xiaoran is a famous idol who has never met him. He does not take it well.
chapters.title: The Dream That Made Zhou Yichen Hug Xiaoran at 3 AM
chapters.epigraph: “The one who knew exactly who Zhou Yichen was.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen rarely remembered his dreams. Most disappeared the moment he woke up. This one didn’t. Unfortunately. The dream started normally. At least—normal by dream standards. He was on campus. Walking toward the media building. Looking for Xiaoran. People started screaming. Not scared screaming. Excited screaming. The kind of screaming usually reserved for celebrities. Yichen stopped. Confused. Then he heard it.

“XIAORAN!”

“LIN XIAORAN!”

“SHE’S HERE!”

Dead silence. Because what? A black van pulled up. Security appeared. Cameras. Hundreds of fans. And out stepped—Lin Xiaoran. Except not his Xiaoran. Well—still his Xiaoran. Different. Much different. Her hair was longer and perfectly styled, her makeup flawless, her clothes designer. Beautiful. Actually breathtaking—the kind of beautiful that made entire crowds stop moving. And apparently—In this dream—she was a famous idol. Dead silence. Dream Yichen was just as confused as real Yichen.

Then Xiaoran smiled. The crowd lost their minds. People screamed louder. Phones everywhere. Security closed in around her. A terrifying realization appeared. Nobody was acting strange. Meaning this was normal. For her. Then Xiaoran walked past him. Completely past him—without stopping, without smiling, without even looking. Like he didn’t exist. Dead silence. That felt awful. Then Yichen followed. Because apparently dream logic said that was acceptable. The next several days became increasingly horrifying.

Because Dream Xiaoran genuinely didn’t know him. Not as a boyfriend, not as a friend, not at all. Meanwhile, Yichen was still himself—still a university student, still a basketball player, still hopelessly in love with her. Only now his girlfriend was an international celebrity who had never met him. Worst dream ever.

Then came the truly evil part. The fan meeting. Because somehow—dream Yichen ended up there. Standing in line like everyone else. Holding merchandise like everyone else. Waiting his turn like everyone else. The humiliation was unbelievable. He reached the table. And there she was. Beautiful, smiling, perfect—and completely unfamiliar.

“Hello.”

Her idol smile appeared—professional, warm, practiced. The one she gave thousands of people. Not the real one. Not his. Somehow that hurt. Then she looked up.

“What’s your name?”

What kind of nightmare was this?

“My…”

His voice actually failed. Dream Xiaoran waited politely. Completely unaware she was destroying him.

“Zhou Yichen.”

She smiled.

“Nice to meet you.”

And that was somehow worse. Much worse. Because no. No it wasn’t. She was supposed to know him. She was supposed to steal his hoodies, send him forty messages a day, hug him out of nowhere while he studied. Not this. Never this. Then Dream Xiaoran signed his album.

“Thank you for supporting me.”

Support. Not boyfriend. Not Yichen. Not idiot. Not mine. Support. The dream became increasingly absurd afterward. Yichen somehow went to her concerts. Watched her interviews. Watched her get more famous, watched millions of people love her—and every single time, she looked right through him like a stranger. Then one day in the dream—things became unbearable. Because an interviewer asked:

“What kind of man is your ideal type?”

Dream Yichen paid very close attention. Obviously. And Xiaoran thought carefully. Then smiled.

“I think someone gentle.”

Good.

“Someone patient.”

Good.

“Someone who makes me feel safe.”

Excellent. Then she laughed.

“I don’t know though. I’ve never met someone like that.”

Dream Yichen almost had a breakdown. WHAT DO YOU MEAN. HE WAS RIGHT THERE. The dream jumped again. Now he stood backstage after a concert. Watching her from a distance. Dream Xiaoran turned. Actually turned. Their eyes met, for the first time. She walked toward him. Closer. Closer. Until she was standing right in front of him. Finally.

“Do I know you?”

The world exploded. Zhou Yichen woke up immediately. 3:17 AM. Dark room. Heart pounding. Genuine irritation. That dream had been cruel. Then he felt something warm and heavy against his side. Lin Xiaoran. They had both fallen asleep on his sofa halfway through a movie, under the same blanket, and she was still there—completely real. Not an idol. Not famous. Not unreachable. Just Xiaoran. His Xiaoran, drooling slightly on his shoulder. Very glamorous.

Yichen stared at her for several seconds. He wrapped both arms around her, tight enough that she made a confused, sleepy noise.

“Hm?”

Half asleep. Barely conscious.

“What happened?”

Nothing. How was he supposed to explain? Sorry, I had a dream where you were a celebrity and didn’t know me, so now I’m emotionally damaged. Impossible. Then Xiaoran opened one eye.

“…Yichen?”

He was still hugging her. Not letting go.

“You okay?”

“…Bad dream.”

Her sleepy expression softened.

“Oh.”

Without even waking up properly, she wrapped her arms around him too.

“There.”

“What.”

“Better.”

Half asleep, and completely unaware she had just fixed everything. Then she yawned. And added:

“You’re my favorite person.”

Sleepy Xiaoran was dangerous. Two seconds later, she was asleep again. Zhou Yichen lay staring at the ceiling, his heart finally calming down. The dream version had been beautiful. World-famous. Perfect. But he preferred this one—the clingy one, the dramatic one, the one who stole his hoodies and never stopped talking. The one who knew exactly who Zhou Yichen was. Before falling asleep again, he tightened his arms around her, just to make sure. In case Dream Xiaoran got any more ideas.

chapters.desc: Jiayi and Ning want a night out by the river. Lin Xiaoran has never been to a club. Zhou Yichen has, exactly twice.
chapters.title: The First Night Out
chapters.epigraph: “Since we were seventeen.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had never been to a club. Not once. Not in high school, when some of her classmates had started sneaking into places with fake confidence and borrowed jackets, and not in her first year at Huaining either, because clubs had always sounded to her like somewhere you went to shout at people you could already text.

Then on Friday afternoon her phone lit up.

Jiayi: We’re going out tonight. The place by the river. Ning’s coming. You’re coming.

Ning: You are actually coming this time.

Xiaoran: What do people even DO there

Jiayi: Dance. Drink. Exist loudly.

Xiaoran: That’s suspiciously vague

Ning: PLEASE

She stared at the screen. She was curious. A little intimidated. Mostly curious. Meilin and Yuhao were at universities hours away now, and Jiayi and Ning were the first friends she’d made here on her own, the two who’d lost her in the festival crowd in her first month and then spent ten frantic minutes looking for her. She wanted to do things with them.

She just didn’t know what to expect. So naturally she rang the person who knew almost everything.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Have you ever been to a club?”

A short pause. “Yes.”

She sat up on her bed. “When?”

“The one by the river? Twice. Once after the spring league final, and once for Fang Ze’s twentieth birthday.”

“You never told me that.”

“I told you both times.” She could hear him smiling. “The first time you were asleep by ten and sent me a sticker of a sleeping panda at eleven. The second time you were up finishing your competition slides and sent me nine stickers and a photo of your face mask.”

She remembered the face mask. She did not remember the club.

“You said the team’s going out.”

“The team went out. To a club. I drove three of them home at half past eleven, because I don’t drink when I’m driving, and I was in bed by midnight.” A pause. “Why?”

“…I’m going tonight. With Jiayi and Ning.”

“Your first time.”

“How do you know?”

“Because you just asked me what people do there.”

“That’s not evidence.”

“It’s fairly convincing evidence.”

She ignored that. “Would you come?”

“Of course.”

She smiled at the ceiling. “Really?”

“Did you think I’d say no?”

“I thought you might have training.”

“Not on a Friday,” said Zhou Yichen. “And not tonight.”

At half past seven he knocked on the door of her studio. Black shirt, dark trousers, the plain watch he always wore. Nothing special. Unfortunately he had the kind of face that made nothing special look expensive.

“How do I look?” She’d chosen a fitted top, a short skirt, boots, a small bag, a little more eyeliner than usual, and an hour on her hair.

He looked at her for a second longer than the question needed. “Beautiful.”

“Just beautiful?”

“Very beautiful.”

“Better.”

Then his eyes went to the bag. “What’s in there?”

“Important things.”

He looked when she opened it. Phone, wallet, lip gloss, powder, a hair tie, a tiny perfume, two packets of tissues, a stuffed panda keyring, and an amount of miscellaneous items that defied classification.

“Are you going to a club or moving house?”

“Don’t judge me.”

He took out the perfume, handed it to her to use now, and put the panda keyring on her desk. “Less in the bag. You’ll put something down somewhere.”

“I’m not that careless.”

He looked at her. She looked back. A few seconds passed.

“…Sometimes.”

He checked that her phone was charged, did up the strap of her bag where it had twisted, and didn’t say one word about the skirt.

“If you feel uncomfortable, tell me. We’ll leave whenever you want. And you don’t have to drink because everyone else does.”

“I know.”

“I know you know,” he said, and held out his hand.

The club was much louder than she’d imagined. The bass came up through the floor into her boots. Lights swung across the ceiling and the dance floor was a single moving animal made of people.

She stopped in the doorway, and he stopped with her.

“Too much?”

“No. Just—” She looked round. “Wow.”

“First impression?”

“Very loud.”

“That’s generally the point.”

Jiayi saw them first and screamed her name across the room, then saw who she’d brought, and her mouth fell open. “You brought the basketball one?”

“My personal guide,” said Xiaoran proudly.

At the bar she spent five minutes reading the menu as if it were an exam paper. “What’s this one?”

“A cocktail.”

“And this?”

“Also a cocktail.”

“What’s the difference?”

“The ingredients.”

“Very helpful,” she said, and he laughed, and then explained properly: which were sweet, which were strong, which tasted like juice and weren’t. He ordered himself water with lemon, because the car was outside. When she chose something pink he put a glass of water beside it without comment.

She took a sip and her eyes went wide. “It tastes like juice.”

“Be careful with those.”

“Why?”

“Some drinks are much stronger than they taste.”

She looked at the glass with deep suspicion. “That’s dishonest.”

“Very,” he agreed.

When the music changed, Jiayi grabbed her hand. “Come and dance.”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

“Go,” he said. “I’ll watch your things.”

At first she was awful. She didn’t know what to do with her hands, wasn’t sure whether she was on the beat, and laughed every time she bumped into someone, which was often. Ning showed her a step. Jiayi showed her another. Somewhere around the third song she stopped thinking about it, and started having fun.

From the edge of the floor, Yichen watched. He wasn’t interested in the dancing. He was interested in the way her face changed every time she got a step right, and the way she looked over her shoulder every minute or two to check he was still there, and lit up every time she found him.

She came back breathless. “I danced.”

“I saw.”

“Was I good?”

“Very.”

“You’re biased.”

“Completely.”

She took his hand. “Come with me.”

He put the water down.

He wasn’t an enthusiastic dancer. He was, unfairly, a good one: one hand at her waist, the other holding hers, moving as if the music were something he’d been told about once and filed away. She stared up at him.

“You can dance.”

“Can I?”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“You never asked,” he said, and bent his head so that she could hear him over the bass. “Stop watching your feet. Follow the music.”

She did. It was much less frightening with him.

Later, sitting in the quiet corner he’d found without seeming to look for it, she studied him over her water.

“How do you know all this? Where the quiet seats are. Which drinks. Where the bathroom is. How to get the bartender’s attention without waving.”

“I’ve been here twice.”

“Twice is not enough to know where the bathroom is.”

“It’s exactly enough to know where the bathroom is.”

She narrowed her eyes. “Did girls come up to you? Those two times?”

There it was. The real question.

“A few.”

“And?”

“And I said I had a girlfriend, and showed them the photo of you in the face mask.”

She gasped. “You did not.”

“Fang Ze has it on his phone. The team manager is quite famous on the team.”

She hid her face in his shoulder, which was where she’d been going to put it anyway. Then she lifted it. “Have you ever brought a girl here?”

He smiled slowly. “I’ve only ever had one girlfriend, Xiaoran. Since we were seventeen. She’s never been to a club before tonight.”

Her cheeks went pink. “…I’m here now.”

“Exactly,” he said, and kissed her forehead, and she forgot her next question.

By midnight she was pleasantly exhausted. Jiayi hugged her at the door and made her promise to come again. Ning took a photograph of the two of them under the sign that Xiaoran made her delete and then made her send.

In the car she leaned back against the seat and turned her head towards him. “I had fun.”

“I know. You’ve been smiling for three hours.”

A few streets later she said, “Did you? Have fun? Even though you were looking after me the whole time?”

He kept his eyes on the road. “I didn’t spend the evening looking after you instead of having fun. I spent it having fun with you.”

She went quiet. Then she reached across the console and took his free hand.

“Next time I want to go with your team.”

“All right.”

“And dance more.”

“All right.”

“And try a different drink.”

“We’ll see.”

“You’re not going to stop me?”

“I’m going to make sure you know what’s in it.”

“Deal.” She thought for a moment. “Wait. Those two times. How long did you stay?”

“About two hours each.”

“And you drove everyone home.”

“Somebody had to.”

“So you’ve been to a club twice, drunk water both times, and gone to bed before midnight.”

“Yes.”

“Zhou Yichen,” she said, delighted, “you’re the most boring man in Shanghai.”

“Probably,” he said. “But tonight I wasn’t bored at all.”

She kissed his cheek at a red light. He drove the rest of the way home with one hand on the wheel and the other holding hers, already certain that tomorrow would bring a very detailed review of everything she’d seen, and at least forty more questions.

He wasn’t complaining. Not even slightly.

chapters.desc: Three rejections in one week, deleted before anyone can ask. She stops saying “guess what” at dinner. He notices.
chapters.title: The Emails She Didn’t Forward
chapters.epigraph: “I made an exception.”
chapters.content:
The first rejection arrived on a Tuesday, at 11:04 in the morning, in the middle of a lecture on audience segmentation.

Dear Ms. Lin, thank you for your interest in our Summer Associate Programme. After careful consideration…

Lin Xiaoran read it under the desk. Then she read the first line again, as if it might have changed its mind.

It hadn’t.

She deleted it.

She looked at the empty space where it had been. Then she looked at the back of the head of the boy in front of her, who was asleep, and at the lecturer, who was explaining the difference between a demographic and a persona as if it might save someone’s life.

Then she went to the deleted folder and deleted it from there too, which felt better, and wrote audience segmentation very neatly at the top of a fresh page, and underlined it twice, and didn’t hear another word for forty minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had applied to nine places.

This had been a sensible number in January. In January she had still been the girl who’d won a national media strategy competition the year before. There had been a trophy shaped like a speech bubble on her shelf and a photograph of her holding it on the faculty noticeboard, and Zhou Yichen had looked at that photograph for so long, every time they walked past it, that Jiayi had started calling it the shrine.

In January, nine applications had felt like nine doors that were already a little bit open.

By the end of March, four of them had said nothing at all.

On the Tuesday, one said no.

On the Thursday, two more did.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Guess what,” said Xiaoran every evening at dinner, normally.

It was how she started. She had started every dinner that way since high school. Guess what, the professor wore odd socks. Guess what, a pigeon walked into the lecture hall and nobody did anything. Guess what, Ning said something so mean to a boy in our group that he apologised to her.

Yichen never guessed. That wasn’t the point. The point was that she said it, and he put his chopsticks down, and she told him.

On Thursday night, at the noodle place behind the sports hall, she didn’t say it.

She told him about the lecture. She told him about Jiayi’s new earrings. She ate all her noodles. She stole two of his dumplings, which was normal, and didn’t make a speech about it, which was not.

He noticed. He didn’t say anything. He moved the dumplings closer to her side of the table.

On Friday she didn’t say it either.

On Saturday he put his chopsticks down before she’d started.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Nothing’s wrong.” She smiled at him. It was a very good smile. She’d practised it in the lift. “I’m tired. Assignments.”

He looked at her for a moment. Then he nodded, and picked his chopsticks up again, and let her have it.

That was the worst part. He believed her, or he let her think he did, and she sat there being believed and felt terrible.

✦ ✦ ✦

The thing was, she couldn’t tell him.

Not because he’d be unkind. He would be the opposite of unkind. He would be so kind it would be unbearable.

He would say their loss. He would say you won a national competition. And then, because he was Zhou Yichen and because his family owned a great many warehouses and knew a great many people, he would say, very carefully, I could ask someone.

And she would have to say no.

She had sat at her grandparents’ table at New Year and listened to Uncle Deng explain, in front of everyone, why a girl from an ordinary family dated a boy like that. She had heard the word he hadn’t quite used. She had held Yichen’s hand under the table so hard her knuckles hurt.

She was not going to get her first internship because somebody knew somebody who knew Mr. Zhou.

So she didn’t tell him. She just stopped saying guess what, because there wasn’t anything to guess.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Thursday night, after the second and third emails, she sat on the stairs outside her studio at midnight, on the fourth floor, because her room felt too small to be disappointed in. She rang Meilin.

Meilin answered on the second ring from a dormitory four hundred kilometres away, sounding exactly as she had at sixteen.

“You only ring at midnight when something’s wrong.”

“Nothing’s wrong.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

So she told her. The nine applications. The three noes. The four silences. The trophy shaped like a speech bubble, which she now couldn’t look at.

Meilin listened to all of it, which was rare, because Meilin usually interrupted by the second sentence.

“Does Yichen know?”

“No.”

“You’re sitting on a staircase at midnight so your boyfriend who lives across the road won’t see your face.”

“…Maybe.”

“Xiaoran,” said Meilin, in the voice she’d used in the noodle shop the winter before, the one that had made the four of them promise not to drift. “You’re not scared he’ll fix it. You’re scared he’ll see you lose.”

Xiaoran didn’t answer. A moth knocked against the stair light.

“He’s seen you lose before,” said Meilin. “He watched you get forty-three in maths. He stayed.”

Xiaoran laughed, which hurt, and went back inside, and didn’t tell him the next day either.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ning found out first, because Ning found out everything.

“You’ve been refreshing your email like it owes you money,” she said on Monday, in the library, without looking up from her own laptop.

“I’m checking for a group assignment.”

“We don’t have a group assignment.”

“Then I’m checking for nothing.”

Ning turned her screen round. On it was the Summer Associate Programme page of a large agency in the financial district, with a large red banner across the top that said APPLICATIONS CLOSED.

“They rejected me too,” said Ning. “On Tuesday. I laughed for ten minutes. Did they reject you?”

Xiaoran looked at her.

“And two others,” she said, very quietly. “And four haven’t answered.”

Ning considered this.

“Does Captain Zhou know?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because he’d fix it.”

Ning was quiet for longer than usual. Then she said, “He can’t fix it. He’s a business student. They don’t even know what a content calendar is.”

Xiaoran laughed, a little wetly, into her sleeve, and Ning pushed a packet of tissues across the desk without comment, which was the kindest thing Sun Ning had ever done in public.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found out on Wednesday.

Not from Ning. Ning would have died first.

He found out because Xiaoran came out of a one-to-one with her portfolio tutor and walked straight into the campus café, and straight through it, and into the bathroom at the back, and stayed there for nineteen minutes.

He knew it was nineteen minutes because he was sitting at their table by the window waiting for her, the way he did every Wednesday at four, with her milk tea already bought and going warm.

When she came out her eyes were red and she had powdered over it, badly, and she sat down and picked up the milk tea and said, “Sorry. Long queue.”

There was no queue. There was never a queue. There was one bathroom and he had watched the door the entire time.

He didn’t say that.

He said, “Okay.”

She drank half her milk tea through the straw without breathing.

He waited.

He was very, very good at waiting. He had waited for her outside exam halls and dressing rooms and once, memorably, outside a bookshop for an hour and ten minutes while she read the first chapter of nine different novels to decide which one she deserved.

“My tutor says my portfolio’s too safe,” she said, to the milk tea. “She says I win competitions because I’m good at telling a panel what it wants to hear, and agencies can smell that. She says I should send them something I’m scared of.”

“Is that why you were in the bathroom?”

“No.” She put the cup down. “I was in the bathroom because three companies have said no and four haven’t bothered and I haven’t told you, and I didn’t want you to find out from my face.”

Silence.

Then he said, “Which three?”

She told him.

He nodded slowly, as if she’d given him a list of patients and he was deciding which to see first. He didn’t say their loss. He didn’t say you won a national competition.

He said, “And you didn’t tell me because you thought I’d ask someone.”

She looked up.

“How do you know that?”

“Because I thought about it on Saturday,” said Yichen. “When you didn’t say guess what. I thought, if it’s what I think it is, I know three people I could call. And then I thought, she’d never forgive me.”

Her mouth opened.

“You knew on Saturday?”

“I guessed on Saturday.”

“You never guess! That’s the whole point! You never guess!”

“I made an exception,” he said.

She stared at him across the table with her ruined powder and her half a milk tea, and then she started laughing, and then the laugh turned into something else halfway through, and she put her face down on her folded arms on the table and cried properly, in the middle of the campus café, at four in the afternoon.

He didn’t come round the table. He reached across it and put his hand on the back of her head and kept it there, warm and still, until she’d finished.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I’m not calling anyone,” he said later, walking her home. “I want you to know that first.”

“Good.”

“Not my father. Not my father’s friends. Not my father’s friends’ daughters, who all work in marketing, apparently, and all went to the same famous university.”

“How do you know that?”

“My mother tells me. Every holiday.”

She snorted.

“But I’ll do one thing,” he said. “If you let me.”

“What?”

“Your tutor said send something you’re scared of.” He stopped at the bottom of her stairs. “What are you scared of?”

She thought about it.

Then she told him.

There was a campaign she had never shown anyone. Not the competition one, all neat charts and audience personas. A real one. For the old noodle shop near their high school, the one with the soft menu and the owner who still gave her milk instead of chili. She’d made it last winter, after she’d sat in that shop with Meilin and Yuhao and been afraid for the first time that the four of them would drift apart. Photographs. A short video. Copy written in the owner’s own words. It was messy and sentimental and it wasn’t strategic at all.

“It’s embarrassing,” she said.

“Is it good?”

She hesitated.

“…It’s the best thing I’ve made.”

“Then send that,” said Yichen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He kept his word. He didn’t call anyone.

What he did was worse.

He became, for nine days, the most unpleasant mock interviewer in the history of Huaining University.

“Why should we hire you instead of the other two hundred applicants?”

“Because I’m—”

“Don’t say passionate.”

“I wasn’t going to say passionate.”

“You were going to say passionate.”

“…I was going to say passionate.”

“Everyone says passionate. Again.”

He sat at his desk in a shirt with the sleeves rolled up, looking at her over his laptop as if she were a quarterly forecast that didn’t add up, and asked her the worst questions he could find. What’s your biggest weakness. Tell me about a time you failed. Why do you want to work in a city where you don’t know anyone. Why should we believe a competition win wasn’t luck.

On the fourth evening she said “passionate” by accident and he simply looked at her over the laptop until she threw a cushion at him. On the sixth she cried halfway through tell me about a time you failed, because the honest answer was this week, and he waited, and when she’d finished he said, “That. Say that. But without the crying,” and she laughed so hard she couldn’t breathe.

The last one made her so angry she answered it perfectly.

He wrote something down.

“What did you write?”

“Nothing.”

She leaned over the desk and looked. He had written that one and underlined it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the tenth day she rewrote the noodle shop campaign for the fourth time and sent it, with a new cover letter, to a media company in Beijing that she had found at one in the morning and not mentioned to anyone. Not to Ning. Not to Jiayi.

Not to Yichen.

It wasn’t a secret, exactly.

It was just that if it said no, she wanted to be the only one who knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three weeks later she was sitting cross-legged on his bed on a Thursday evening with her laptop on her knees, pretending to edit a group presentation, when the email came in.

She saw the company name.

Her stomach did something complicated.

Yichen was at his desk with a textbook open, reading the same page he’d been reading for twenty minutes because she’d been humming.

She opened the email.

She read the first line.

She read it again, very slowly, as if it were in a language she’d only just learned.

Then she read the whole thing three times, and opened two more tabs to check the company was real, and that the programme was real, and that she was real, and looked at the address at the bottom, which was in Beijing, more than a thousand kilometres from this bed and this boy and this terrible, wonderful, too-quiet room.

She looked up at him.

He was still reading the same page.

She took a breath.

“Yichen.”

chapters.desc: A summer internship in Beijing. A training camp outside the city. Eight weeks and more than a thousand kilometres.
chapters.title: The Internship in Another City
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t want you to go tomorrow.”
chapters.content:
The first time Lin Xiaoran mentioned Beijing, Zhou Yichen thought she was talking about a drama.

She was sitting cross-legged on his bed, laptop balanced on her thighs, hair tied into a messy ponytail. There were three open tabs on her screen, a half-finished cup of milk tea beside her, and an expression he had learned to recognize.

Excitement.

The kind that made her forget to blink.

“Yichen.”

He looked up from his textbook. “Hm?”

“I got an offer.”

His eyes moved to her face. “For what?”

She turned the laptop around.

A media company in Beijing. A summer internship program. Eight weeks. A competitive placement, with opportunities to work on real campaigns, assist with production, and contribute to editorial projects.

He read the page carefully.

Then he looked at her.

“Xiaoran.”

“I know.”

“You got it?”

“I got it.”

He closed his textbook.

For a moment, she thought he might say something practical. Ask about accommodation, the company, the schedule, whether she had checked the transportation arrangements.

Instead, he smiled.

A proper smile.

“Congratulations.”

Her face brightened. “Really?”

“Why would I not congratulate you?”

“I don’t know. Maybe because it’s in Beijing.”

He glanced at the laptop again. “It’s a good opportunity.”

“It’s very far.”

“I know.”

“Eight weeks.”

“I can read.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re not helping.”

He reached over and gently tugged the end of her ponytail.

“I’m trying to understand why you’re looking at me like I’ve personally arranged for Beijing to be on the other side of the country.”

“You could have arranged for it to be closer.”

“Unfortunately, my influence has limits.”

She laughed, and he pulled her closer by the waist, pressing a kiss against her temple.

He was genuinely happy for her.

He knew how much work she had put into building her portfolio, from last year’s competition to the two campaign samples she had rewritten four times since. He remembered the nights she had stayed up revising projects, the frustration when her first applications went unanswered, and the way she had pretended not to care when a company rejected her.

This was something she had earned.

He wasn’t going to make her feel guilty for receiving it.

But later that night, when Xiaoran had fallen asleep beside him, he found himself looking at the internship page again.

Eight weeks.

Beijing.

He calculated the distance without meaning to.

Then he locked his phone and turned toward her.

She was sleeping with one hand curled near her cheek, her hair scattered across his pillow. He gently moved a strand away from her face.

“Eight weeks,” he whispered.

She didn’t hear him.

He kissed her forehead anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

The training camp call came three days later.

Yichen was in the university gym when his coach asked him to stay behind after practice.

The invitation was for a summer training camp outside the city. A chance to train with a more competitive group, work with experienced coaches, and potentially secure a place in a larger university-level tournament roster. Coaches from other programmes usually came to watch the final week.

It was the kind of opportunity he had been working toward since joining the basketball team.

He listened, asked a few questions, and accepted.

When he told Xiaoran, she was sitting across from him in a café, enthusiastically explaining the internship’s orientation schedule.

She stopped mid-sentence.

“Wait.”

He looked at her.

“Training camp?”

“Mm.”

“When?”

“Same period as your internship.”

She stared at him.

He nodded.

For a few seconds, neither of them spoke.

Then Xiaoran slowly lowered her straw.

“So we’re both leaving.”

“Looks like it.”

“Different cities.”

“Yes.”

“For almost two months.”

“Eight weeks.”

She gave him a wounded look. “Why are you repeating the number?”

“Because you keep asking.”

“Maybe I’m hoping you’ll say something different.”

He reached across the table and touched her fingers.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked down at their hands.

“It’s a good opportunity for you,” he said. “And the training camp is important to me.”

“I know.”

“Then we should go.”

She nodded.

It was the reasonable answer.

The correct answer.

The answer they would both have given if they were discussing anyone else’s relationship.

But she didn’t smile.

And he noticed.

✦ ✦ ✦

They spent the next two weeks preparing for their separate departures.

Xiaoran researched accommodation, transportation, nearby convenience stores, and the safest routes between her apartment and the company. She made a spreadsheet with far too many tabs. Yichen checked the details with her, pointed out two things she had overlooked, and helped her compare the available options.

He even accompanied her to buy luggage.

She chose a pale blue suitcase.

He thought it was too small.

She thought he was being dramatic.

They compromised by buying a slightly larger one.

At the training camp, Yichen would be staying in shared accommodation with the other players. He packed his sportswear, shoes, recovery equipment, and a few personal belongings.

Xiaoran watched him fold his clothes.

“You’re very efficient.”

“Someone has to be.”

“I packed my suitcase yesterday.”

“You packed it three times.”

“Because I kept remembering things.”

“You brought four pairs of shoes.”

“They’re different.”

“They’re all white.”

She looked offended. “They are not.”

He glanced at the suitcase.

She followed his gaze.

“Fine. Three are white.”

He smiled.

She threw a T-shirt at him.

He caught it easily.

For all their teasing, the packing days were strangely difficult.

They had always been together in the small, ordinary ways that made a relationship feel effortless. A quick visit after class. Dinner after practice. A message asking whether the other had eaten. A hand reaching across a table without needing to ask.

Now, every small thing seemed to have an ending attached to it.

The last time they would shop together before leaving.

The last dinner at their usual place.

The last evening studying in the same room.

The last night she could fall asleep with her head against his shoulder.

Neither of them said it aloud.

✦ ✦ ✦

The night before Xiaoran’s flight, she went to Yichen’s apartment.

She arrived with a small paper bag.

“What’s that?” he asked.

“Something for you.”

He took it.

Inside was a compact photo album.

Not an expensive one. Just a simple little book with photographs she had printed over the past few months.

Their first university basketball game. A picture of him looking away while she took a photograph. A café receipt with a ridiculous doodle she had drawn. A photo of them in Chengdu, standing in front of the panda enclosure. A blurry picture of his hand holding hers inside a car.

There were captions written in her handwriting.

Some were silly.

Some were embarrassingly sentimental.

He turned each page slowly.

At the end, there was a small note.

For when you miss me. Which will probably be often, because I’m very lovable.

He looked at her.

She was suddenly very interested in the sleeve of her sweater.

“It’s not a big gift.”

“Xiaoran.”

“You don’t have to say anything. It’s just something I thought—”

He closed the album and set it carefully on the table.

Then he pulled her into his arms.

She went willingly, pressing her cheek against his chest.

“Thank you,” he murmured.

“You like it?”

“I love it.”

“Really?”

He leaned back just enough to look at her.

“I’ll take it with me.”

She smiled.

Then, after a moment, her expression softened.

“Don’t lose it.”

“I won’t.”

“Don’t let your teammates borrow it.”

“Why would they borrow my photo album?”

“I don’t know. Maybe they’ll want to see how pretty your girlfriend is.”

He laughed quietly.

“Very confident.”

“It’s a fact.”

He kissed her forehead.

She closed her eyes.

For a while, they stayed like that, holding each other in the quiet apartment.

Eventually, she whispered, “I’m going to miss you.”

His arms tightened slightly.

“I know.”

“That’s all?”

He lowered his head, his cheek brushing her hair.

“I’m going to miss you too.”

She pulled away to look at him.

“That’s still not enough.”

He studied her face for a second.

Then he cupped her cheek.

“I don’t want you to go tomorrow.”

Her expression changed.

He rarely said things like that.

Not because he didn’t feel them, but because he usually preferred to make her feel secure rather than burden her with everything he was thinking.

But tonight, he was tired of pretending the distance was something he could simply calculate and manage.

“I know you should go,” he continued. “I know it’s important. And I want you to have it.”

She swallowed.

“But I don’t want you to go.”

Her eyes became glossy.

“Yichen…”

He brushed his thumb beneath her eye before a tear could fall.

“I’m not asking you to stay.”

“I know.”

“I just want you to know that wanting you here and wanting you to succeed aren’t mutually exclusive.”

That was when she finally cried.

Not loudly. Not dramatically.

Just a few tears she couldn’t quite stop.

Yichen pulled her back against him.

“Hey.”

“I’m fine.”

“You’re crying on my shirt.”

“Then don’t wear such a nice shirt.”

He let out a small breath of laughter, kissing the top of her head.

“That’s my solution?”

“It’s a very practical one.”

He held her until she stopped trying to hide her tears.

✦ ✦ ✦

The airport was worse than either of them expected.

Xiaoran had insisted she was going to be fine.

She had said it while brushing her teeth, while checking her ID card, while eating breakfast, and again in the car.

By the time they reached the departure hall, she had become unusually quiet.

Yichen pulled her suitcase beside him.

“Have you checked everything?”

“ID card, phone, wallet, charger.”

“Laptop?”

“Yes.”

“Internship documents?”

“Yes.”

“Medicine?”

She nodded.

“Good.”

She looked up at him.

“You sound like my father.”

“Your father probably has excellent judgment.”

“Don’t agree with me.”

He smiled faintly.

They stood near the entrance to the security area.

People moved around them, dragging suitcases and talking on their phones. Announcements echoed overhead.

Xiaoran looked at the entrance.

Then at him.

Then back at the entrance.

“Can you come with me?”

“I can accompany you to the security line.”

“I mean…”

She stopped.

He understood.

He stepped closer and wrapped his arms around her.

She buried her face against his chest.

“I don’t want to leave you.”

His hand moved slowly over her back.

“I know.”

“What if I get lonely?”

“Call me.”

“What if you’re training?”

“I’ll call you back.”

“What if I’m busy?”

“Then I’ll wait.”

“What if—”

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up.

He touched her cheek.

“We’ll figure it out.”

She nodded, but her lips trembled.

He leaned down and kissed her forehead.

Then her left cheek.

Then her right.

Finally, he kissed her lips, gently and without rushing, as if he were trying to give her something to carry with her.

When he pulled away, she held onto his jacket.

“Don’t forget me.”

His expression changed.

For the first time that morning, he looked almost offended.

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You think eight weeks is enough to make me forget you?”

She tried to smile.

He lowered his forehead to hers.

“I’ve spent years getting used to having you around. I’m not going to suddenly become unfamiliar with you because you’re in another city.”

She nodded.

“Okay.”

“Go make something of this opportunity.”

She sniffed.

“Okay.”

“And eat properly.”

“Okay.”

“Don’t skip meals because you’re busy.”

“Okay.”

“Don’t walk around with your phone out in unfamiliar places.”

“Okay.”

“Don’t—”

She pressed a finger against his lips.

“I’m going to miss you even more if you keep giving me homework.”

He kissed her fingertip.

“Then go.”

She hugged him one last time.

And when she finally walked toward security, she turned around twice.

He was still there both times.

The third time, he raised his hand.

She waved.

Then she disappeared into the crowd.

Yichen remained where he was for a little longer than necessary.

His phone vibrated.

Xiaoran: Don’t look so handsome when I leave. It’s unfair.

He looked at the message.

A small smile appeared.

Yichen: I’ll try to look worse next time.

Xiaoran: You can’t. It’s genetic.

He laughed under his breath.

Then he put his phone away and went home.

The apartment was quiet.

Her cup was still on the table.

A hair tie was on the sofa.

One of her slippers had somehow ended up beneath his desk.

He picked it up and placed it beside the other one.

Then he opened the little photo album.

He looked at the first photograph for a long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first week was easy.

Or at least, they tried to make it easy.

Xiaoran sent him photographs of Beijing.

The office building.

The view from her apartment.

A bowl of noodles she claimed was the best thing she had ever eaten.

A photograph of herself wearing her internship identification card, looking very pleased with her own reflection.

Xiaoran: Do I look professional?

Yichen: Very.

Xiaoran: Really?

Yichen: You look like someone who knows what she’s doing.

Xiaoran: I don’t.

Yichen: They don’t need to know that.

She laughed at her phone in the middle of the office.

He sent her pictures of the training camp in return.

The court.

His teammates.

A photograph of his shoes after practice.

She complained that he was terrible at taking pictures.

He told her that he was documenting his surroundings, not producing a magazine.

Their video calls were frequent.

Sometimes they spoke for an hour.

Sometimes only ten minutes.

Sometimes Xiaoran would call him while walking home, and he would stay on the line until she reached her apartment.

She would tell him about the people she met, the projects she was assigned, the things she learned.

He would tell her about practice, his teammates, the training schedule, and the coach who seemed to believe that sleep was a privilege rather than a biological necessity.

They were busy.

But they were happy.

Until the second week.

It happened on a Thursday.

Xiaoran had been working on a campaign proposal for most of the day. Her supervisor had asked her to revise several sections, and she had stayed late to finish the changes.

By the time she got back to her apartment, it was nearly ten.

She showered, ate something small, and called Yichen.

No answer.

She assumed he was still training.

She sent a message.

Xiaoran: Are you done?

No reply.

She changed into her pajamas and sat on the bed.

Then she opened their chat again.

Still nothing.

She knew he was busy.

She knew the training camp was demanding.

She knew he couldn’t always answer.

But she missed him.

That was all.

She wanted to hear him say her name.

She wanted to complain about her supervisor, tell him about the ridiculous coffee machine at work, and ask whether he had eaten.

She wanted to hear his voice.

At 10:47 p.m., her phone finally rang.

She answered immediately.

“Yichen?”

“Sorry.”

His voice sounded tired.

She sat up. “It’s okay. Are you done?”

“Just finished.”

“Did you eat?”

“Mm.”

“What did you eat?”

“Dinner.”

She frowned. “That’s not an answer.”

He gave a quiet laugh.

“Rice, chicken, vegetables. Happy?”

“Very.”

There was a pause.

Then he asked, “How was your day?”

She opened her mouth.

And suddenly, she didn’t know where to start.

She had been waiting all evening to tell him everything. But now that he was finally there, she could hear the exhaustion in his voice.

“Fine,” she said.

“Just fine?”

“Mm.”

“Anything interesting?”

She looked down at her blanket.

“Not really.”

He was quiet for a moment.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hmm?”

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Then sleep early.”

She nodded, although he couldn’t see her.

“Okay.”

“I’ll call you tomorrow.”

“Okay.”

“Goodnight.”

“Goodnight.”

The call ended.

She stared at the screen.

It had been less than four minutes.

She knew he was tired.

She knew he had done nothing wrong.

Still, the disappointment settled in her chest.

She put her phone down and turned off the light.

For the first time since arriving in Beijing, she cried herself to sleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next few days were worse.

Not because anything terrible happened.

That was the problem.

Nothing terrible happened.

Xiaoran continued going to work. She completed her assignments, attended meetings, learned how to navigate the city, and gradually became more comfortable with her colleagues.

Yichen continued training.

His schedule became more intense as the camp approached its final evaluation. There were additional sessions, recovery work, and team meetings.

Their calls became shorter.

Their messages became less frequent.

They still said good morning.

They still said goodnight.

They still told each other to eat.

But something had changed.

Xiaoran stopped sending him every little thing.

She stopped taking photographs of her lunch just to show him.

She stopped calling him when she walked home.

When something funny happened, she sometimes opened their chat, typed a message, and deleted it.

She didn’t want to become another responsibility in his day.

Yichen noticed.

Of course he noticed.

He knew her habits too well.

He knew that when Xiaoran was excited, she sent messages in clusters. When she was annoyed, she sent voice notes. When she was sleepy, she used fewer punctuation marks.

And when she was trying not to bother him, she became excessively considerate.

It was the last one that worried him.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday night, he called her after practice.

She answered after several rings.

“Hello?”

“Busy?”

“No. I was just washing my hair.”

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Rice.”

“With?”

She paused.

“Food.”

He closed his eyes briefly.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I’m asking because I care, not because I’m conducting an investigation.”

She laughed softly.

“I had beef noodles.”

“Good.”

There was a silence.

He sat on the edge of his bed, phone against his ear.

“How was your week?”

“Good.”

“Work?”

“Good.”

“Your supervisor?”

“Good.”

He leaned forward, resting his elbows on his knees.

“You’ve become very fond of that word.”

She smiled faintly.

“It’s a useful word.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I’m really okay.”

“I didn’t say you weren’t.”

She looked out of the window.

The city lights blurred slightly.

“I just don’t want you to worry.”

His jaw tightened.

“Why would I not worry?”

“Because you’re busy.”

“I’m aware of my schedule.”

“And the training camp is important.”

“So is your internship.”

She didn’t answer.

He waited.

Then, quietly, he asked, “Are you lonely?”

Her eyes stung.

She wanted to say no.

She wanted to be mature about it. She wanted to be the girlfriend who supported him without needing anything in return.

But she was tired of being mature.

“A little,” she admitted.

His expression softened.

“How little?”

She laughed weakly.

“Quite a lot.”

He leaned back against the wall.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because I know you’re tired.”

“I’m tired, Xiaoran. I’m not unavailable.”

She pressed her lips together.

“I don’t want you to feel like you have to call me.”

“I don’t.”

“Or like you have to make time for me.”

“I want to make time for you.”

“Yichen…”

“Listen to me.”

His voice was gentle, but firm enough to make her stop.

“You’re not asking me to abandon training. You’re asking your boyfriend to spend time with you.”

She looked down.

“That’s different?”

“Very.”

A tear slipped down her cheek.

He exhaled slowly.

“Are you crying?”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Maybe.”

He closed his eyes.

He hated being unable to reach her.

He hated that there were more than a thousand kilometres between them, that he couldn’t take her face in his hands, couldn’t wipe the tears away, couldn’t pull her against his chest and let her complain until she felt better.

“Show me your face,” he said.

She turned on her camera.

Her eyes were red.

He stared at her for a moment.

Then he smiled gently.

“Hello, pretty girl.”

She sniffed.

“Don’t.”

“Why?”

“I’m crying.”

“I can see that.”

“Then don’t call me pretty.”

“Would you prefer I call you a disaster?”

She laughed despite herself.

“Better,” he murmured.

Her smile faded again.

“I miss you.”

His gaze softened.

“I miss you too.”

“I miss you so much.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t.”

He was quiet.

Then he said, “You’re right. I probably don’t know exactly how much.”

She looked at him.

“But I know that when I finish training, the first thing I do is check my phone to see whether you’ve messaged me. I know that I keep looking at the time because I want to know whether you’re awake. And I know that I have been sleeping with your ridiculous photo album beside my bed.”

Her lips parted.

He glanced away for a moment, almost embarrassed by his own confession.

“Is that enough evidence?”

She covered her mouth.

“Yichen…”

“I’m not asking you to pretend this is easy.”

He looked directly into the camera.

“It’s not easy for me either.”

chapters.desc: Shorter calls, one missed night that matters, and a station where this time she’s the one waiting.
chapters.title: The Internship in Another City (Part 2)
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t make yourself smaller just because I’m far away.”
chapters.content:
The next week, they tried something different.

They stopped treating their calls like appointments that had to be squeezed into the end of the day.

Instead, they began sharing their ordinary lives again.

Yichen would send her a photograph of his breakfast before practice.

Xiaoran would send him a voice note while walking to work.

He would call her for five minutes during his lunch break, even if all he had to say was that the training session had been exhausting.

She would send him a photograph of the sky outside her office.

Sometimes they didn’t even have anything to say.

They simply stayed on the phone while doing their own things.

One evening, Xiaoran was working on a presentation when Yichen called.

“Hi.”

“Hi.”

“What are you doing?”

“Working.”

“Still?”

“Almost done.”

He heard the sound of her keyboard.

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

She told him.

He was quiet for a moment.

Then he said, “I miss you.”

Her fingers stopped.

She looked at the phone.

“Why are you saying that suddenly?”

“Because I do.”

She smiled at the screen.

“I miss you too.”

“Come here.”

She blinked.

“What?”

“Come here.”

She looked at the phone again.

“Yichen, we’re on a video call.”

“I know.”

She laughed.

“Then how?”

“Use your imagination.”

She leaned toward the camera and pressed a kiss against the screen.

He watched her.

Then he smiled.

“That’s not very convincing.”

“It’s all you get.”

“Unfortunate.”

She laughed again.

And for the first time in days, the distance felt a little less cruel.

✦ ✦ ✦

But the hardest moment came during the sixth week.

Xiaoran had been selected to assist with a presentation for a major client.

It was a small role, but a meaningful one. She had worked hard on the research and was excited about the opportunity.

She wanted to tell Yichen.

She wanted him to be proud of her.
